subcategories.label: Bacterial leaf spot
subcategories.description: Brown or yellow spots on leaves during humid summer weather. Cosmetic only — rarely affects rhizome health. Improve air circulation by thinning crowded clumps. Severe: copper-based fungicide if needed.

seasonNotes.4: Bloom opens. Same borer watch as the blue flag — larvae tunnelling inside the leaf bases.
seasonNotes.5: Bloom finishes, and this is the one to cut promptly. The pods ripen, split and float seed around the pond; it spreads far more freely than the native.
seasonNotes.6: Fat ribbed green capsules stand where the flowers were. Take them off before they brown and split.
seasonNotes.7: Divide crowded clumps.
seasonNotes.10: Cut back to about six inches above the water after frost.

photos.caption: Yellow flag along the pond edge at the end of April.

plants.name: Butterfly Weed
plants.guide: The butterfly weed on the property is a native milkweed that does well in these well-drained mountain soils. Bright orange flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) bloom June through August and are magnets for monarchs, swallowtails, and a wide range of native bees. Drought-tolerant once established — it resents wet feet and overwatering. Slow to emerge in spring; do not assume it has died and disturb the root. The deep taproot makes transplanting difficult, so site carefully.
plants.soilNotes: Perfectly matched to Hayesville//native soils — well-drained acidic sandy loam is ideal. Butterfly weed is native to dry rocky/sandy slopes and will rot in poorly drained heavy clay. On flat areas at Church Mountain Road where clay Bt subsoil impedes drainage, raised beds or high spots are strongly preferred. pH 6.0–7.0 is optimal; native soils at ~5.0 may benefit from a light lime amendment. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun — at least 6 hours of direct sun daily. South or west-facing open slopes are best. The species is native to dry open meadows and roadsides; it will decline in shade or with root competition from trees.
plants.frostSensitivity: Extremely cold-hardy (Zone 3). No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road. Very late to emerge in spring — do not disturb the crown before late April; emergence at ~2,873 ft elevation can be delayed until mid-May.

prune.description: Cut back last year's dead stems to ground level in late winter/early spring before new growth emerges. Do not cut back in fall — the dead stems provide winter habitat for native solitary bees. In early spring, check for bright orange-red shoots emerging at soil level before cutting.

subcategories.label: Seed
subcategories.peakWindow: Oct 1–20 — collect pods just as they split
subcategories.description: Collect seed pods in fall when they begin to split and before the silky floss carries seeds away. Cold stratification (30–60 days at 34–38°F in moist sand or paper towel) dramatically improves germination. Sow outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or stratify in the fridge and start indoors in March. Seedlings take 2–3 years to bloom.

subcategories.label: Root cuttings
subcategories.peakWindow: Mar — before growth begins
subcategories.description: Root cuttings are the most reliable vegetative method. Take 3–4 inch sections of root in late winter/early spring before emergence. Plant horizontally 1–2 inches deep. Roots are thick and brittle — work carefully. Plants grown from root cuttings typically bloom in 1–2 years.

fertilize.description: Do not fertilize. Butterfly weed evolved in poor, dry soils — excess nitrogen produces lush weak foliage that is more aphid-susceptible and fewer flowers. If plants are in good, well-drained soil, no supplemental fertilizer is needed or desirable.

water.description: Water weekly during the first year to establish the taproot. Once established (year 2+), butterfly weed is drought-tolerant and performs better with less water. Overwatering or waterlogged conditions will kill the plant. At Church Mountain Road, established plants should need no supplemental watering except during extended summer droughts.

repot.description: Not applicable — the deep taproot makes transplanting very difficult. Site carefully from the start.

subcategories.label: Aphid infestation
subcategories.peakWindow: May–Jun when new growth is most vulnerable
subcategories.description: CONFIRMED ISSUE at Church Mountain Road (May 2026): black aphid infestation with severe distortion and curling of growing tips. Small black dots on stems and leaves are the aphids or their frass. Do NOT use systemic insecticides — monarch caterpillars feed on these plants and would be killed. Management: (1) strong blast of water to knock aphids off; (2) insecticidal soap sprayed directly on affected areas; (3) tolerate moderate infestations — lady beetles and parasitic wasps often bring populations under control naturally within 2–3 weeks. Distorted growth will not recover; new growth after control should come in clean.

seasonNotes.2: Cut last year's dead stems to the ground before anything emerges. Root cuttings, if you want more, come out of the same visit.
seasonNotes.4: Slow to wake — at this elevation it can hold off until mid-month, so don't dig where you think it died. Black aphids hit the new tips hard here; that's confirmed on this property, not a hypothetical.
seasonNotes.5: Orange starts. Water weekly through the first year while the taproot goes down; after that it would rather be left dry.
seasonNotes.7: Bloom winding down. Keep an eye on the tips for aphid distortion.
seasonNotes.9: Collect pods as they start to split, before the floss carries the seed off.

plants.name: Summer Cascade Wisteria
plants.guide: The Summer Cascade® wisteria on the property is a cultivar of Kentucky wisteria — a native North American species that does not share the invasive habits of Asian wisterias. Long cascading racemes of purple-dark lavender flowers bloom in June and again lightly through summer. Vigorous climber to 15–20 ft — needs a strong pergola, arbor, or trellis. Fragrant and deer-resistant. Unlike Asian wisterias, it blooms reliably without the 7–10 year wait.
plants.soilNotes: Adaptable to Hayesville//soils across a wide pH range (6.0–8.0). Prefers well-drained soil but tolerates occasional wet periods better than many vines. Avoid wet clay subsoil areas where root rot can occur. Mulch the root zone to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun — minimum 6 hours. South or west-facing fence or pergola is ideal for maximum bloom. Partial shade reduces flowering significantly. At Church Mountain Road, an open south-facing exposure will produce the best bloom.
plants.frostSensitivity: Very cold-hardy (Zone 4). No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road. As a native species, it is far better adapted to fluctuating early spring temperatures than Asian wisterias.

subcategories.label: Summer trim (after bloom)
subcategories.peakWindow: Late Jun–Jul — after first bloom flush
subcategories.description: After the main June bloom flush, cut back long whippy shoots to 5–6 leaves. This controls size, tidies the plant, and encourages secondary flower bud formation for later flushes. Do not cut back into the main framework at this time.

subcategories.label: Hard winter pruning
subcategories.peakWindow: Feb 1–20 before bud swell
subcategories.description: Late winter is the main structural pruning window. Cut back all lateral side shoots to 2–3 buds from the main framework. This concentrates energy into bloom rather than foliage and keeps the plant manageable. Also the time to train new shoots along the support structure.

propagate.description: Simple or serpentine layering in spring. Pin a flexible young shoot to the ground, wound the underside lightly, cover with soil. Roots form in 2–4 months; sever from parent the following spring. Most reliable vegetative method for home gardeners.

fertilize.description: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers entirely — they promote lush foliage at the expense of flowers. If soil is very poor, a low-nitrogen fertilizer (e.g., 5-10-10) can be applied in late winter/early spring. Church Mountain Road native soils are generally adequate; most established wisterias need no fertilizing.

water.description: Water regularly during the first two years to establish a deep root system. Once established, wisteria is reasonably drought-tolerant. Consistent moisture during bloom development (May–June) supports a heavier flower display. Mulch the root zone to retain soil moisture.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape vine.

subcategories.label: Support structure integrity
subcategories.description: Check support structure in late winter before growth begins and again in fall. A mature wisteria exerts significant weight and leverage on trellises and pergolas. Ensure posts, anchors, and wires are secure. Wooden structures may need periodic reinforcing as the vine matures.

subcategories.label: Scale insects
subcategories.description: Look for small bumpy brown or white waxy scales on stems and older wood. Dormant oil spray in late winter/early spring (before bud break) is the most effective control. In summer, look for crawlers on new growth — insecticidal soap or neem oil when crawlers are active.

bloom.window: Late spring, then repeat flushes through summer
bloom.note: A summer-blooming native wisteria — reblooms after the first flush, unlike the aggressive Asian kinds.

seasonNotes.1: The main structural cut — laterals back to two or three buds off the framework. Check the support while the vine is bare; a mature one pulls hard.
seasonNotes.3: Leafing out fast. Tie new shoots where you want them while they're still soft enough to direct.
seasonNotes.4: The first flush opens toward the end of the month, a week or two behind valley plants.
seasonNotes.6: After the main flush, cut the long whippy shoots back to five or six leaves. That's what keeps it in bounds and encourages the repeat.
seasonNotes.9: Check the support again before winter loading.

plants.name: Elpis Clematis
plants.guide: The Elpis clematis here is a repeat-blooming large-flowered hybrid that puts up blooms from spring through fall. Grows 6–8 ft tall by 2–3 ft wide on a trellis or fence — ideal for vertical interest in mixed borders or against structures. Large flowers are a draw for bees and butterflies. Classic rule: 'feet in the shade, head in the sun' — shade the root zone with mulch or low plants while letting the top climb into full light.
plants.soilNotes: Requires well-drained soil amended with organic matter. Hayesville//soils are adequate but benefit from generous compost amendment at planting. A slightly higher pH (6.5–7.0) than the native soil's 4.5–5.5 may be beneficial — a light lime application at planting is worthwhile. Avoid waterlogging — clematis wilt is more severe in poorly drained soils. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to part shade. East-facing positions with morning sun and afternoon shade are ideal at Church Mountain Road — afternoon summer sun can scorch leaves and stress the plant. Keep roots shaded with 2–3 inches of mulch regardless of sun exposure.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4. No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road. May emerge a bit later than valley plants in spring — do not cut back too early in spring before checking for live buds.

prune.description: Elpis blooms on both old and new wood (Group 2). Can be left largely unpruned (just clean out dead stems) for early blooms on old wood, or cut back lightly (by 1/3 to 1/2) in early spring for a tidy plant with vigorous bloom. Remove all dead and damaged stems first, then decide how hard to cut back based on amount of live wood. Full renovation cuts in alternate years help maintain vigor.

propagate.peakWindow: Jun — internode cuttings when stems are semi-ripe
propagate.description: Take 3–4 inch internode cuttings (just below a leaf node) in late spring/early summer when stems are semi-ripe. Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and root in perlite/peat mix under mist or in a plastic-covered propagator. Keep shaded and humid; rooting takes 4–6 weeks. May be protected by plant patents — check before propagating for distribution.

fertilize.peakWindow: Mar — before active growth; Jun — after first bloom flush
fertilize.description: Clematis are heavy feeders. Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10) in early spring before growth begins, and a potassium-rich liquid fertilizer (e.g., tomato feed) after the first bloom flush to promote continued repeat blooming through summer. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds in late summer — they promote soft growth vulnerable to late-season disease.

water.description: Regular, consistent moisture is essential — clematis dislikes both drought and waterlogging. Mulch the root zone heavily (2–3 inches) to keep roots cool and moist. During hot dry spells in summer, deep watering 2–3 times per week may be needed. Drip irrigation or soaker hose at the base is ideal — keep foliage dry to reduce disease risk.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape vine.

subcategories.label: Clematis wilt
subcategories.peakWindow: May–Jun — most common in cool wet springs
subcategories.description: Sudden wilting and blackening of stems, often starting at a leaf node and moving rapidly up or down the stem. Cut affected stems back to healthy tissue immediately and discard (do not compost). Disinfect pruners between cuts. Plants almost always recover from below-ground buds — do not assume the plant is dead. Improve air circulation and avoid wetting foliage.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on foliage during warm humid periods. More cosmetic than damaging at moderate levels. Improve air circulation. Potassium bicarbonate spray or neem oil controls light infestations. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizing which promotes susceptible soft growth.

seasonNotes.1: Clean out dead stems and little else. It flowers on both old and new wood, so it forgives a light hand better than a hard one.
seasonNotes.4: Tie the new shoots in gently — the stems are brittle and snap in wind. Sudden blackening of a stem is wilt; cut it out at the base.
seasonNotes.5: Bloom opens and runs through the summer. A heavy feeder — a second feed after the first flush pays for itself.
seasonNotes.7: Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist. A white film on the foliage in humid weather is mostly cosmetic.
seasonNotes.9: Still flowering if the fall is mild. Don't cut it back early next spring before checking for live buds.

plants.name: DreamCloud Reblooming Hydrangea
plants.guide: The DreamCloud® hydrangea on the property is part of the Endless Summer® series — a reblooming bigleaf that puts up large bright white mophead flowers on both old and new wood from early summer through fall. The reblooming habit is the key advantage over traditional bigleafs: even if old-wood buds are lost to a late frost or winter damage, new-wood buds form and bloom through the growing season. Pure white flowers hold their color well in partial shade.
plants.soilNotes: Prefers moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Hayesville//soils at Church Mountain Road are acidic (4.5–5.5) — DreamCloud flowers white regardless of pH, unlike blue/pink bigleafs. Amend planting hole with generous compost. Avoid low spots with standing water or heavy clay subsoil that stays wet in winter. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Part sun to part shade. East-facing positions with morning sun and afternoon shade are ideal at Church Mountain Road — afternoon summer sun can scorch leaves and stress the plant. North-facing exposures also work well. Avoid full hot south or west exposure without supplemental water.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4 overall, but old-wood flower buds are vulnerable. At ~2,873 ft elevation, late frosts through mid-May can damage or kill buds formed on last year's growth — a real risk at Church Mountain Road. The reblooming genetics mean the plant will still flower on new wood, but the first bloom flush may be delayed. Protect with frost cloth during late spring freeze events if possible.

prune.peakWindow: Mar — after last hard freeze, before bud swell
prune.description: Prune conservatively in late winter — remove only clearly dead wood (brown, dried stems with no live buds). Do not cut back healthy stems as they carry the first bloom buds. After the first bloom flush (late June–July), lightly deadhead spent flowers and remove any weak or crossing stems. Full renovation cuts (to near ground level) can be done in late winter every 3–4 years to rejuvenate old plants, accepting one season of reduced bloom.

propagate.description: Take 4–5 inch tip cuttings from non-flowering stems in early summer. Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and stick in a perlite/peat mix. Keep shaded and consistently moist. Rooting takes 4–6 weeks. May be protected by plant patents — check before propagating for distribution.

fertilize.description: Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10 or azalea/rhododendron fertilizer) in early spring as growth begins. A second light application in May before bloom promotes strong flower development. Avoid fertilizing after July — late-season nitrogen promotes soft growth more susceptible to frost damage.

water.description: Bigleaf hydrangeas are among the most moisture-demanding landscape shrubs. Water deeply 2–3 times per week during hot dry stretches. Morning watering is preferred; avoid wetting foliage in the evening. Mulch 2–3 inches around the base to retain moisture and keep roots cool. At Church Mountain Road, the cooler climate and higher rainfall reduce stress compared to valley sites, but supplemental water is still needed during dry stretches.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces during warm, humid weather — common in late summer at Church Mountain Road. Primarily cosmetic. Improve air circulation around the plant. Potassium bicarbonate or neem oil spray for control if severe. Avoid overhead watering.

subcategories.label: Botrytis blight
subcategories.description: Gray fuzzy mold on flowers and buds during cool, damp weather — spring and fall are peak windows at this elevation. Remove and dispose of affected flower heads. Improve air circulation. Fungicide treatment rarely needed in landscape settings.

subcategories.label: Late frost bud damage
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr–early May — critical watch period at ~2,873 ft elevation
subcategories.description: Old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. Check the 10-day forecast in April and early May. When a hard frost (<28°F) is predicted, cover with frost cloth or old bedsheets overnight. Even with bud loss, the reblooming genetics ensure bloom on new wood later in the season.

bloom.note: A reblooming bigleaf — flowers on both old and new wood, so a late frost won't cost the whole show.

seasonNotes.2: Prune conservatively — dead wood only, nothing carrying live buds. Feed as it wakes.
seasonNotes.3: The critical frost watch. Old-wood buds stay vulnerable into early May here; if a freeze is forecast, frost cloth is worth the trouble. Cool damp weather can bring grey mould on the buds.
seasonNotes.5: First bloom, later than the valley. If a late freeze took the old-wood buds, don't panic — it reblooms on new wood, just delayed.
seasonNotes.7: Deep watering two or three times a week in heat; these are the thirstiest shrubs on the place. Powdery mildew starts in late summer.
seasonNotes.9: The rebloom flush carries on into fall.

plants.name: Pop Star Endless Summer Reblooming Hydrangea
plants.guide: The Pop Star hydrangea is a compact reblooming bigleaf that produces abundant lacey blue or pink mophead flowers on both old and new wood from early summer through fall. The reblooming habit is the defining trait — even if a late spring frost damages old-wood flower buds, new buds develop and bloom through the growing season. Flower color is soil pH dependent: acidic soils (4.5–5.5) yield blue; alkaline soils (above 7.0) yield pink. At Church Mountain Road's native pH, expect blue flowers without amendment. Low-maintenance, pollinator magnet, electric color in the landscape.
plants.soilNotes: Thrives in Hayesville//soils at Church Mountain Road. The native acidic pH (4.5–5.5) is ideal for blue flowers — no lime amendment needed. Bigleaf hydrangeas demand moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Amend the planting hole generously with compost at establishment. Avoid low spots with standing water or heavy clay subsoil that stays wet in winter — root rot is the enemy. On flat areas at the property where clay Bt argillic subsoil impedes drainage, use a raised or bermed bed position. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Part sun to part shade. East-facing positions with morning sun and afternoon shade are ideal at Church Mountain Road — afternoon summer sun can scorch leaves and stress the plant, reducing bloom. North-facing exposures work but may reduce flowering by 20–30%. Avoid hot south or west exposures without supplemental irrigation during July–September dry stretches. The property's east-facing mid-slope positions are textbook hydrangea habitat.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4 overall, but old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. At ~2,873 ft elevation, the May 1–21 window is the critical frost-risk period for buds on last year's growth — a real concern at Church Mountain Road. The reblooming genetics mean the plant will still flower on new wood even if old-wood buds are lost, but the first bloom flush may be delayed or reduced. Protect with frost cloth during late spring freeze events if possible, or site in the thermal belt mid-slope position where frost risk is slightly lower than in hollows.

prune.peakWindow: Mar — after last hard freeze, before bud swell
prune.description: Prune conservatively in late winter (Feb–early Mar, before bud swell). Remove only clearly dead wood (brown, dried stems with no live buds). Do not cut back healthy stems as they carry the first bloom buds. At Church Mountain Road elevation, last hard freeze typically occurs around mid-April, so hold off major pruning until late February to March to avoid hitting it. After the first bloom flush (late June–July), lightly deadhead spent flower clusters and remove any weak or crossing stems. Full renovation cuts (to near ground level) can be done in late winter every 3–4 years to rejuvenate old plants, accepting one season of reduced bloom.

propagate.description: Take 4–5 inch tip cuttings from non-flowering stems in early summer (Jun–Jul). Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and stick in a perlite/peat mix. Keep shaded and consistently moist. Rooting takes 4–6 weeks. The Pop Star cultivar may be protected by plant patents — check before propagating for distribution.

fertilize.description: Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10 or azalea/rhododendron formulation) in early spring (Mar) as growth begins. A second lighter application in May before bloom promotes strong flower development. Avoid fertilizing after July — late-season nitrogen promotes soft growth more susceptible to frost damage. At Church Mountain Road's native soil pH, the azalea-specific formulations are ideal as they include micronutrients suited to acidic mountain soils.

water.description: Bigleaf hydrangeas are among the most moisture-demanding landscape shrubs. Water deeply 2–3 times per week during hot dry stretches (June–September). Morning watering is preferred; avoid wetting foliage in the evening. Mulch 2–3 inches around the base to retain moisture and keep roots cool. At Church Mountain Road, the cooler mountain climate and higher rainfall (estimated 62–68 in/yr at elevation) reduce stress compared to lowland sites, but supplemental water is still critical during the July–August dry window when afternoon thunderstorms can be sporadic.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces during warm humid weather — common in late summer at Church Mountain Road when RH climbs to 70–90%. Primarily cosmetic but worth managing. Improve air circulation around the plant. Potassium bicarbonate or neem oil spray for control if severe. Avoid overhead watering — wet foliage in evening promotes the disease.

subcategories.label: Botrytis blight
subcategories.description: Gray fuzzy mold on flowers and buds during cool, damp weather — spring (March–April) and fall (September–October) are peak windows at this elevation. Remove and dispose of affected flower heads. Improve air circulation. Fungicide treatment rarely needed in landscape settings.

subcategories.label: Late frost old-wood bud damage
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr–early May — critical watch period at ~2,873 ft elevation
subcategories.description: Old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. At Church Mountain Road, check the 10-day forecast in April and early May. When a hard frost (<28°F) is predicted, consider covering with frost cloth or old bedsheets overnight. Even with old-wood bud loss, the reblooming genetics ensure strong bloom on new wood later in the season — this is the insurance policy built into the variety.

bloom.note: Endless Summer type — reblooms continuously on new wood once established.

seasonNotes.2: Dead wood only, before the buds swell. Feed at the same time.
seasonNotes.3: Frost-watch season for the old-wood buds; the risk runs into the third week of May at this elevation. It reblooms on new wood regardless, so a loss delays the show rather than cancelling it.
seasonNotes.5: The first flush opens, about a week behind valley plants.
seasonNotes.7: Water deeply and often. Humid stretches bring a powdery film to the leaves.
seasonNotes.9: Still going, which is the whole point of the type.

plants.name: Spiderwort
plants.guide: The spiderwort on the property is a native eastern wildflower at home in moist woodland edges and dappled shade — exactly the habitat Church Mountain Road offers. The three-petaled purple-blue flowers open in morning and close by afternoon, but the plant produces new buds continuously through late spring and early summer. Extremely low-maintenance once established; spreads by self-seeding and underground rhizomes. Totally harmless to wildlife and pets. The common name references the spidery quality of the stamens and the thread-like leaf bases.
plants.soilNotes: Ideally suited to Church Mountain Road's Hayesville//soils. Prefers moist, well-drained loam rich in organic matter at pH 5.5–7.0 — the native slightly acidic (4.5–5.5) mountain soils are acceptable, especially when amended with compost or leaf mulch. Tolerates seasonal wet feet better than many woodland plants but despises permanently waterlogged clay subsoil. Established plants are reasonably drought-tolerant once their rhizomes are deep, but spring through early summer moisture (when actively flowering and setting seed) is critical for the best display. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Partial shade to dappled sun — north and east-facing woodland edges are ideal at Church Mountain Road. Morning sun with afternoon shade from the forest canopy is the sweet spot. Too much afternoon heat and bright sun causes the flowers to wilt and close early in the day. Full shade reduces flowering significantly. The moist woodland edge habitat at this elevation is perfect — the plant does not thrive in hot, dry, full-sun locations even with irrigation.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 3 — extremely cold-tolerant. No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road elevation. The foliage emerges in late April at ~2,873 ft (about 1–2 weeks later than lowland Georgia) and can handle a late frost without damage. The emerging shoots are soft and bright green but recover quickly from frost. Established rhizomes are completely frost-proof and persist through winter.

prune.peakWindow: May 20–Jun 15 — as first flush of flowers begins to fade
prune.description: Deadheading extends bloom significantly — remove spent flowers just below the flower head on the stem to prevent seed formation and redirect energy into new bud development. At Church Mountain Road elevation, deadheading through early June maintains peak flowering. After late June as temperatures rise and daylength peaks, deadheading becomes less critical and the plant's energy naturally shifts toward seed production and vegetative growth. Optional: cut back the entire plant (stems and foliage) to 6 inches after the main bloom window ends in mid-to-late June — this encourages fresh new growth and sometimes produces a secondary lighter bloom flush in late summer or early fall.

propagate.peakWindow: Sep–Oct seed collection; early spring division
propagate.description: Two methods: (1) Division — in early spring (Mar–Apr) before active growth or in fall (Aug–Sep) after bloom, carefully dig and separate the rhizome-connected plantlets. Each piece with roots and a fan of leaves will establish quickly if replanted immediately at the same depth and kept consistently moist for the first season. (2) Seed — let mature seedpods dry on the plant through summer; collect in September–October and direct-sow in a prepared bed or cold frame. Seed germinates readily without stratification if given moisture and cool nights (fall sowing is most reliable). Seedlings appear in spring and reach flowering size in 1–2 years. The property's native soil supports self-seeding naturally — volunteers often appear nearby if you leave flowers unmulched.

fertilize.peakWindow: Mar–Apr before active growth; May–early Jun before peak bloom
fertilize.description: Light hand. Early spring (Mar–Apr) with a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., Plant-tone or 10-10-10) awakens the plant after dormancy. A second light application in late April–early May supports robust flowering. Church Mountain Road's naturally organic-matter-rich soil and annual leaf mulch additions usually provide sufficient nutrition — over-fertilizing produces lush foliage at the expense of flowers and promotes weak growth susceptible to fungal disease in humid conditions. If plants are yellowing or obviously stunted, a soil test through UGA Extension is worth the $9.

water.description: Critical April through early July when actively flowering and setting seed. Deep soaking once a week beats daily light watering — the goal is moist but not waterlogged soil. At Church Mountain Road's estimated 62–68 in/yr precipitation (valley baseline 57 in plus 5–15% orographic lift), established plants in good drainage rarely need supplemental summer water except during drought stretches. Spring through early June is the priority window — consistent moisture at this time ensures peak bloom and good seed set. Apply 2–3 inches of leaf-litter mulch year-round to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature.

repot.description: Not applicable — spiderwort is a landscape perennial, not a container plant.

inspect.description: Generally pest- and disease-free. In very humid summers (Church Mountain Road's 70–90% summer RH), watch for leaf spot diseases or occasional powdery mildew on lower foliage — mostly cosmetic. Improve air circulation by removing lower spent leaves and avoiding overhead watering. The plant is rarely bothered by insects. If slugs damage the emerging foliage in spring, apply iron-phosphate bait (Sluggo) around the base in April.

bloom.note: Each flower lasts a morning; the plant opens fresh ones for weeks.

seasonNotes.3: Foliage comes up a week or two behind lowland Georgia. The soft new shoots shrug off a late frost.
seasonNotes.4: Bloom starts. Each flower lasts a morning and it opens fresh ones for weeks — deadheading below the head keeps that going.
seasonNotes.5: As heat and daylength build, bloom slows. That's the plant, not a problem.
seasonNotes.6: Cutting it back hard after bloom often brings a tidy second flush of foliage.
seasonNotes.8: Division or seed collection, depending on which you want more of.

plants.name: Creeping Fig
plants.guide: Creeping fig is a tender evergreen climbing fig — small, leathery heart-shaped leaves on wiry stems that cling to walls and supports by aerial rootlets. By the book it's only reliably hardy to about Zone 8, so at 2,873 ft you'd expect it to be a tender seasonal here — but ours has proven otherwise. The plant on the property came through the winter outdoors and leafed back out the following spring (Mom noticed it returning in spring 2026), so on its sheltered footing it's earning a permanent spot rather than living as a one-season annual. Give it part shade and steady moisture through the warm months and it flushes happily. Help it through the cold — a deep mulch over the roots and a cover on the hardest nights — and there's good reason to expect it back each spring. Taking a few cuttings in late summer is still worth doing as cheap insurance.
plants.soilNotes: Wants moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and does NOT like to dry out — the opposite of the property's drought-tolerant natives like the butterfly weed. The native Hayesville//acidic loams suit it fine as long as moisture stays steady; mulch to hold water. In a container, use a rich potting mix that still drains freely. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Part shade to filtered sun. Protect it from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind — a sheltered east-facing wall or a spot under high shade gives it the best summer. Deep shade slows it; blazing exposure scorches the thin leaves.
plants.frostSensitivity: Tender by the book — reliably hardy only to about Zone 8 on paper, with foliage that can take damage in the upper 20s°F. At 2,873 ft in Zone 6b that would normally make it a gamble outdoors, but the plant here has already proven it can take a winter on this property: it came back in spring 2026 after the previous winter. Treat it as tender-but-established rather than doomed, and give it the help that keeps it that way — a deep mulch (4–6 in) mounded over the roots and crown before hard cold sets in, and a frost cloth, old sheet, or cardboard draped over the top growth on the coldest nights (single digits / hard sustained freezes). A sheltered, out-of-the-wind footing against a wall is what tips the odds its way here. A few late-summer cuttings are still worth taking as insurance, but on current evidence this one earns a permanent place.

prune.description: Pinch and trim during active warm-season growth to encourage branching and keep it tidy on its support. It's vigorous when warm, so light, frequent tip-pinching beats one hard cut. Hold off in the cold months — let it rest, and wait until spring growth resumes to clean up any winter-burned tips rather than cutting them off in fall.

subcategories.label: Stem cuttings (overwintering)
subcategories.peakWindow: Aug–early Sep, well before first frost
subcategories.description: Cheap insurance rather than a necessity, now that the outdoor plant has wintered over here. Take 3–5 inch stem cuttings in late summer, before frost — they root very easily, in water or a moist, free-draining mix. Pot up the rooted cuttings and overwinter them on a bright indoor windowsill as a backup, then plant out after the May frost date if you want to spread it to a new spot.

fertilize.description: Light feeding during the active warm season supports the summer flush — a balanced liquid feed every few weeks is plenty. Ease off by late summer so you're not pushing soft growth right as you take cuttings. No feeding outdoors in the cold months.

water.description: Keep evenly moist all through the warm season — creeping fig does not tolerate drying out, and the thin leaves wilt fast in heat. Water more in hot, dry spells and mulch around the roots to hold moisture. Container plants dry out quickest — check them often.

repot.description: Only relevant if you're growing it in a pot to lift in and out. Refresh or step up the pot in early spring as the overwintered plant comes back into growth, before setting it outside after the frost date.

subcategories.label: Winter protection
subcategories.peakWindow: mid Oct–Nov — get protection on before hard cold
subcategories.description: Not a pest watch — this is about helping it through the cold. Our plant has wintered over outdoors here, and the way to keep it doing so is to get protection on before the hard freezes: mound 4–6 inches of mulch over the roots and crown in mid-to-late autumn, and keep a frost cloth or sheet handy to drape over the top growth on the coldest nights. If the top does burn back in a brutal winter, don't pull it — wait for spring and it may well push fresh growth from the protected crown.

subcategories.label: Indoor pests (if overwintered)
subcategories.description: Only relevant if you're keeping cuttings or a potted backup indoors over winter. Indoors, creeping fig is prone to the usual dry-air houseplant pests — scale, mealybug, and especially spider mites in heated rooms. Keep humidity up, check leaf undersides, and treat early with insecticidal soap.

seasonNotes.3: Refresh or step up the pot if it's container-grown, as growth restarts.
seasonNotes.5: Full warm-season growth — the good stretch. Pinch and trim to keep it branching on its support.
seasonNotes.7: Take a few stem cuttings as insurance. It has wintered over here, so this is cheap belt-and-braces rather than a rescue.
seasonNotes.9: Get the protection on before hard cold — deep mulch mounded over the roots and crown, and something draped over the top growth on the worst nights.
seasonNotes.11: If you're keeping a potted backup inside, watch it for scale and mites. Indoors is where they find it.

plants.name: Turf Grass
plants.guide: The mowed turf below the house is the one piece of ground here run as turf rather than meadow — kept green, even, and close-cut. Turf-type tall fescue is the grass for it: a cool-season bunchgrass that's the standard choice for North Georgia lawns and an even better fit at this elevation, where the summers run too cool for Bermuda and far too humid for the creeping bentgrass a golf course would use. (The “autumn bentgrass” Mom flagged is a different plant entirely — a native meadow grass, not a turf.) Fescue grows in clumps rather than running, so it never knits over bare spots on its own; the clearing stays lush because the thin places get overseeded every fall, not because any one season is allowed to slide.
plants.soilNotes: Native ground here is acidic (pH 4.5–5.5); fescue wants 6.0–6.5, so a fall application of dolomitic lime — sized to a UGA soil test, not guessed — is the single biggest lever on turf color. The Hayesville//loams drain well on the slope. Retest every three years. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun on the open, south-facing clearing — ideal light for fescue. The same exposure that melts frost and greens the clearing first in spring also dries it fastest in a summer drought, so summer water lands here before anywhere else on the property.
plants.frostSensitivity: Cool-season grass: greens up early, holds color late, and shrugs off light frost and snow. Its hard season is summer, not winter — deep heat and humidity, not cold, are what stress it. Hardy well past the property's Zone 6b winters.

mow.description: Mow high — 3 to 3.5 inches — and never take off more than a third of the blade in one pass. Tall fescue holds color and crowds out weeds when it's cut tall; scalp it and you invite crabgrass and disease. Raise the deck to 3.5–4″ through the June–August heat so the longer blades shade the roots and slow brown patch. Leave the clippings — they return free nitrogen. Keep the mower blade sharp; a torn tip browns and stresses the plant.

propagate.peakWindow: Sep 1–25 — the one window that matters
propagate.description: Tall fescue is a bunchgrass — it grows in clumps and won't spread to fill bare spots on its own, so the turf stays full only if you overseed thin areas every fall. September beats spring by far: the seed roots through two cool seasons before it ever faces summer. Rake or scratch the soil, sow turf-type tall fescue seed (about 5–6 lb per 1,000 sq ft on bare ground, 3–4 to thicken existing turf), and keep the top inch moist until it germinates in one to two weeks. Avoid spring seeding — young fescue rarely survives its first mountain summer.

subcategories.label: Fall feeding
subcategories.peakWindow: Sep 15 & again early Nov
subcategories.description: Fall is when fescue does its real growing, and where almost all the year's nitrogen belongs. Feed once in mid-September as it wakes from summer, and again in early November to build roots for winter. A UGA soil test sizes the rate; in general, a slow-release lawn fertilizer at the label rate. Never push heavy nitrogen in spring or summer — it forces soft growth straight into brown-patch weather.

subcategories.label: Lime (soil-test driven)
subcategories.peakWindow: Oct–Nov, by soil test
subcategories.description: Native ground here runs acidic (pH 4.5–5.5); fescue wants 6.0–6.5. Dolomitic lime is slow to react, so a fall application gets the whole winter to work. Size it to a UGA Extension soil test (Pickens County, 706-253-8840, ~$9) rather than guessing — over-liming is as bad as none. Retest every three years.

subcategories.label: Light spring green-up
subcategories.peakWindow: Mar — light only
subcategories.description: At most a light feeding in March to green it up. Keep it modest — the fall feedings do the heavy lifting, and spring nitrogen mostly fuels disease and extra mowing.

subcategories.label: Summer survival
subcategories.peakWindow: Jun–Aug — ~1″/week
subcategories.description: In a dry mountain summer, water deeply and infrequently — about one inch a week including rain, in the early morning so the blades dry before night and dodge disease. The open south-facing clearing dries fastest of any ground on the property. Established fescue can also be left to go semi-dormant and brown in drought; it greens back up with the fall rains.

subcategories.label: New-seeding establishment
subcategories.peakWindow: Sep–Oct, until rooted
subcategories.description: Fresh September seed is the exception to deep-and-infrequent: keep the top inch of soil moist with short, frequent waterings until the seedlings are up and rooted — roughly two to three weeks — then taper back to the normal weekly soak.

subcategories.label: Brown patch watch
subcategories.peakWindow: Jun–Aug, humid heat
subcategories.description: Brown patch is fescue's main trouble here — roughly circular patches of tan, collapsed blades that appear in hot, humid stretches, worst where the lawn stays wet overnight. Manage it culturally first: water in the morning not the evening, raise the mowing height, hold off nitrogen, and improve airflow. Reach for a fungicide only if an outbreak is severe and spreading.

subcategories.label: Weeds
subcategories.peakWindow: Late Feb–Mar — crabgrass pre-emergent
subcategories.description: The key pre-emergent timing is for crabgrass — put it down before the soil warms through the mid-50s°F, which at this elevation runs late February into March (about when the forsythia blooms). Spot-treat broadleaf weeds in fall, when they're easiest to knock back and the fescue is growing strongly enough to fill in behind them.

seasonNotes.1: Crabgrass pre-emergent goes down before the soil warms through the mid-50s. Get ahead of it rather than chasing it.
seasonNotes.2: A light green-up feed at most. The fall feedings do the real work.
seasonNotes.4: Peak growth. Mow tall — three to three and a half inches — and leave the clippings. Hold the nitrogen; soft blades walking into summer is how brown patch starts.
seasonNotes.6: Brown patch weather: roughly circular patches of tan collapsed blades in humid heat. About an inch of water a week, early morning, deep and infrequent.
seasonNotes.8: The window that matters. Fescue is a bunchgrass and won't fill bare spots on its own, so overseeding is what keeps the clearing thick. Keep the top inch moist until it roots, and feed while you're at it.
seasonNotes.10: Second feeding, and lime if the soil test calls for it — the native ground here runs acidic.

plants.name: Meadow Grass
plants.guide: Beyond the mowed turf, the rest of the clearing is run the opposite way — as meadow. It's cut back hard just once a year and otherwise left to grow tall and loose. This is where the native warm-season bunchgrasses belong: little bluestem, switchgrass, indiangrass, and the autumn bentgrass Mom flagged for the property, threaded through with wildflowers. The contrast is the whole point — a crisp, close-mown turf reading against a tall, seed-headed, pollinator-fed meadow. It also asks almost nothing in return: no lime, no fertilizer, no weekly mowing.
plants.soilNotes: Leave it acidic and unlimed — the native grasses and wildflowers are adapted to the property's natural pH (4.5–5.5). No fertilizer: feeding a meadow favors weeds and floppy, lodging growth over the wildflowers you actually want.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun, the same south-facing clearing as the turf — warm-season natives thrive in it. Drier upland spots suit little bluestem and indiangrass; the damp lower edge toward the spring drainage suits switchgrass and the autumn bentgrass.
plants.frostSensitivity: Warm-season grasses — they green late in spring and go dormant gold after fall frost, which is exactly the look you want. The standing dead growth gives winter structure and cover until the late-winter cut.

mow.peakWindow: Late Feb — one cut, before green-up
mow.description: Mow once a year in late winter, down to about 4–6 inches — never lower — to clear the previous season's dead growth before the new one starts and before ground-nesting birds get going. That single cut is the whole maintenance rhythm. The exception is establishment: in the first year of a newly seeded meadow, mow every 4–6 weeks at that same height through the season to hold back annual weeds while the slow native perennials root in, then drop to the once-a-year cut from year two on.

observedGrasses.note: Two distinct grasses seen across the turf and meadow. A first read from photos only — NOT confirmed on the ground. To be settled by Mom's own pictures down the road (a seed-head in August is the clincher).

varieties.label: The coarse clumping grass
varieties.basis: wide, heavily-veined blades in a bunch from one crown; consistent with the turf canon already names
varieties.confirmBy: ligule + clumping habit on the ground

varieties.label: The low, spreading grass
varieties.inferredId: Possibly crabgrass (Digitaria sp.) — a summer annual
varieties.basis: flat, star-shaped spread of light-green blades over thin/bare soil in mid-summer
varieties.confirmBy: finger-like (digitate) seed spikes appearing in August

seasonNotes.1: The one cut of the year, down to four to six inches and never lower, before green-up.
seasonNotes.4: Coming up for the season. Leave it be.
seasonNotes.7: Grasses and wildflowers doing their work — feeding pollinators, setting seed. Nothing to do.
seasonNotes.10: Dormant gold, and that's the look. The standing growth is winter structure and cover until the late-winter cut.

plants.name: Lizard's Tail
plants.guide: Lizard's Tail is a native wetland perennial of the southeastern US, typically found in shallow water or moist soil at pond and stream margins. The plant produces heart-shaped leaves and distinctive nodding white flower spikes that give it the common name. At Church Mountain Road, it is planted in soil adjacent to the pond rather than in standing water — a drier siting than its native habitat, though the proximity to the water table keeps it consistently moist.
plants.soilNotes: Saururus cernuus is native to swamp margins and shallow water but thrives in moist soil away from standing water. Church Mountain Road's Hayesville/soils in the pond-adjacent bed — acidic sandy loam to loam at pH 4.5–5.5 — are well-matched if the soil stays consistently moist through summer. The plant's shallow root system demands organic matter; mulch 2–3 inches with leaf litter or compost. Avoid any spot where drainage is so perfect the soil dries in summer heat. [SOIL SERIES UNCONFIRMED: no soil test has ever been run here; the series once named in this note were falsified for this elevation. Treat pH and texture as inferred, never as measured.]
plants.aspectPreference: Part shade to full shade. Saururus is native to the dappled understory of bottomland hardwood forests — the pond-margin setting here, especially if it receives morning light and afternoon shade from surrounding trees, is ideal. Direct hot afternoon sun will stress the plant unless soil moisture is absolutely consistent.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4. No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road elevation. The above-ground foliage dies completely to the ground after first hard frost (typically October–November at ~2,873 ft); the rhizome survives dormant in the soil and re-sprouts in spring.

prune.description: Cut back dead foliage after the first hard frost flattens the leaves. At Church Mountain Road elevation, this runs late October through November. Remove all above-ground growth down to the crown to tidy the pond edge and reduce overwintering pest habitat. Spring cleanup is also fine — either approach works. Do not cut back in fall and leave the dead stems; the plant prefers a clean cut-back.

propagate.description: Divide rhizomes in early spring (March–April) just as new shoots begin to emerge. Lift the entire clump, separate by hand into sections carrying 2–3 emerging buds and healthy roots, and replant immediately in moist soil. Alternatively, allow the plant to spread naturally — the rhizomes will creep through moist soil and fill the area over 2–3 seasons. This plant is self-spreading by rhizome in the right conditions.

fertilize.description: Light feeding in early spring (April) with a balanced slow-release fertilizer. Saururus evolved in rich organic bottomland soils — annual compost top-dressing (1–2 inches) is more valuable than synthetic fertilizer. Most established plants in consistently moist soil with decent organic matter need no supplemental feeding.

water.description: Consistent moisture is non-negotiable. At Church Mountain Road's pond-adjacent siting, the proximity to the water table likely keeps the plant satisfied through summer, but watch for any prolonged dry spell — if rainfall is light, deep watering once weekly in July–August is prudent. The shallow rhizome system dries quickly in full sun; afternoon shade helps reduce water stress.

repot.description: Not applicable — Saururus is a landscape perennial, not a container plant.

inspect.description: Monitor for signs of stress if any extended dry period occurs mid-summer. Wilting or yellowing foliage in July–August (when the plant should be vigorous) signals inadequate moisture. Check for slugs or other defoliating insects in damp pond-edge habitat — they are attracted to the moist soil. Lizard's Tail itself is quite pest-resistant; problems are usually cultural (drought or waterlogging).

bloom.note: Curved white flower spikes over the pond edge.

seasonNotes.3: A light spring feed as it starts moving. It evolved in rich organic muck, so it isn't shy about it.
seasonNotes.5: Curved white spikes over the pond edge. Timing here is still being established — worth noting when they actually open.
seasonNotes.7: Consistent moisture is non-negotiable. Wilting or yellowing in a dry mid-summer stretch is the signal.
seasonNotes.10: Foliage blackens and dies to the ground after the first hard frost; the rhizome carries it over.

plants.name: Crocosmia
plants.guide: A summer torch — arching sprays of red-orange trumpets held over fans of sword-shaped leaves, opening mid-to-late summer just as the hydrangeas wind down. It grows from corms that multiply into clumps and naturalizes readily at this elevation. Hummingbirds work it hard. Wants full sun to light afternoon shade and, above all, well-drained ground.
plants.soilNotes: Fine in the property's acidic sandy loam, but drainage is the make-or-break: corms rot in soggy winter ground. A raised or sloped, free-draining spot is ideal.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun gives the most flowers; a little afternoon shade is fine at elevation. Deep shade leaves it floppy and shy to bloom.
plants.frostSensitivity: Corms are hardy here (roughly to zone 5–6); the top dies back after frost and returns from the corm each spring. In a hard-winter year, a deep mulch over the clump is cheap insurance.

prune.description: Cut the foliage back once frost blackens it (late Oct–Nov), and tidy spent flower spikes through the season. Leave the corms in the ground.

propagate.description: Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years as growth begins in late winter/early spring: lift the chains of corms, separate, and replant the plump top corms. Near-effortless — this is how a single clump becomes a drift.

fertilize.description: A light feed as shoots emerge in spring is plenty; it's not a hungry plant. Go easy on nitrogen or you'll get leaves at the expense of flowers.

water.description: Water through the summer bloom in dry spells. Established clumps are fairly drought-tolerant once the show is over.

repot.description: Not applicable in the ground. Keep an eye that it doesn't overrun neighbors — it spreads.

subcategories.label: Spread / crowding
subcategories.description: Crocosmia naturalizes vigorously. If it starts crowding neighbors, lift and thin the corm chains in spring — the same job as dividing.

subcategories.label: Spider mites
subcategories.description: Hot, dry spells can bring spider mites — fine webbing and pale stippling on the blade-leaves. Hose off forcefully; rarely serious.

bloom.note: Seen in full bloom on the property in mid-July 2026.

seasonNotes.2: Divide congested clumps as growth starts — lift the chains of corms and replant the fat ones.
seasonNotes.4: A light feed as the shoots come up is plenty. Go easy on nitrogen or you'll get leaves instead of flowers.
seasonNotes.6: In flower. Nothing to do but enjoy it — and cut a few stems for the vase, they hold well.
seasonNotes.7: Keep it watered through a hot dry stretch. Fine webbing and pale stippling on the blades means mites.
seasonNotes.9: Cut back once frost has blackened the foliage.

plants.name: Garden Phlox
plants.guide: Tall garden phlox — domed clusters of pink-to-lavender and white flowers on upright stems through mid-to-late summer, sweetly fragrant and a magnet for butterflies and hummingbird moths. A dependable old-garden perennial here. Its one recurring nuisance is powdery mildew in humid stretches, so the whole game is giving it air and watering low.
plants.soilNotes: Happiest in richer, moisture-retentive soil — work compost in and keep it mulched to hold the roots cool and damp. The property's acidic loam suits it.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to light shade. Morning sun with good air movement is the mildew-beating combination; avoid still, damp, crowded corners, which is exactly where mildew takes hold.
plants.frostSensitivity: Fully hardy here (to about zone 4). It dies to the ground in winter and returns from the crown each spring.

subcategories.label: Spring thinning (for airflow)
subcategories.peakWindow: Late Mar–Apr as shoots reach ~6 in
subcategories.description: When the clump is a few inches up, remove about a third of the weakest stems at the base. Fewer, better-spaced stems mean far better air movement — the single most effective thing you can do against powdery mildew.

subcategories.label: Fall cutback
subcategories.description: After frost, cut the stems to the ground and clear the debris away (don't compost mildewed foliage — it re-seeds the problem next year).

propagate.description: Divide the clump every 3–4 years in early spring or early fall to keep it vigorous — lift and split the crown, replant the strong outer pieces. Basal cuttings in spring also root easily.

fertilize.description: Feed in early spring with a balanced slow-release and top-dress with compost; a second light feed in June supports the big bloom. Don't overdo nitrogen — soft, lush growth mildews worst.

water.description: Water deeply at the base in summer dry spells — steady moisture keeps it un-stressed and less mildew-prone. Never water overhead: wet leaves are how mildew spreads.

repot.description: Not applicable — a landscape perennial.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: The recurring one, worse in Jasper's humid summers: a white powdery film on the leaves, seen on the property this year. Manage culturally first — thin for airflow, water low, deadhead, clear fallen leaves. Horticultural oil or a bicarbonate spray helps if severe; over time, favor mildew-resistant divisions.

subcategories.label: Spider mites
subcategories.description: Hot, dry stretches can bring spider mites (fine webbing, stippled leaves). Hose off; keeping the plant well-watered is the best prevention.

bloom.note: Seen blooming on the property in mid-July 2026.

seasonNotes.3: When the clump is a few inches up, take out about a third of the weakest stems at the base. Fewer, better-spaced stems is the whole mildew strategy.
seasonNotes.5: A second light feed supports the long bloom.
seasonNotes.6: In flower, and carrying some powdery mildew most years — that pale dusty film. Mostly cosmetic. Water at the roots rather than overhead, and deadhead the spent trusses to keep it going.
seasonNotes.8: Still blooming. Division works now as well as it does in spring.
seasonNotes.10: Cut to the ground after frost and clear the debris away. Don't compost mildewed foliage — it re-seeds the problem.

plants.name: Panicle Hydrangea
plants.guide: The toughest and most sun-tolerant of the hydrangeas — a big upright shrub carrying elongated cone-shaped flower clusters that open lime-white in mid-summer and age to pink as fall comes on. Because it blooms on NEW wood, it's fully frost-safe and easy: cut it back hard in late winter for bigger heads. The property's specimen is a large, established shrub.
plants.soilNotes: The least fussy hydrangea for the property's acidic loam — tolerates a wider range than the bigleaf types. Soil pH does NOT change its color (that's a bigleaf-only trait). Compost annually.
plants.aspectPreference: Takes more sun than the bigleaf types — full sun to part shade both work at this elevation, and more sun means more and sturdier flower cones. The east and open exposures suit it well.
plants.frostSensitivity: Frost-safe. It blooms on the current season's growth, so it pushes new flower buds every spring regardless of winter cold or late frosts — the dependable bloomer of the group.

prune.description: Late winter (Feb–early Mar), before growth starts. Cut back hard to a strong low framework — the harder you cut, the bigger the flower heads (though fewer of them). It blooms on new wood, so this won't cost you any flowers.

propagate.description: Softwood tip cuttings in early summer root readily under a humidity dome in 3–4 weeks. Ground layering works too — pin a low branch to the soil and walk away.

fertilize.description: A balanced slow-release in early spring, optionally a second light feed in early June. Don't overfeed — floppy stems that can't hold the big cones are usually too much nitrogen.

water.description: Deep weekly watering through summer, especially while the cones are forming and opening. More drought-tolerant than the bigleaf types once established, but the flowers are better with steady moisture.

repot.description: Not applicable — a landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Flopping / support
subcategories.description: Heavy flower cones after summer rain can pull branches down. If it flops, cut for the vase or lightly stake; over time a harder late-winter prune builds sturdier stems.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: Less prone than the bigleaf types, but humid stretches can still bring a light powdery film. Mostly cosmetic; improve airflow if it recurs.

bloom.note: Opens lime-white and ages to pink; seen coming into bloom on the property in mid-July 2026. Mom confirmed it in flower on the ground 2026-07-18 (Mama's Perspective — her third answer; independent second witness to the bloom window).

seasonNotes.1: Cut it back hard while it's still dormant, down to a strong low framework. It blooms on new wood, so the harder you cut the stronger the cones.
seasonNotes.3: Balanced slow-release. Don't overfeed — floppy stems can't hold the big cones.
seasonNotes.5: Cones start forming. Softwood tip cuttings root readily under a dome if you want another.
seasonNotes.6: Cones filling out lime-green to white. Mom confirmed it in flower here in mid-July 2026. Deep weekly water while they're opening; otherwise nothing to do but watch.
seasonNotes.7: Heavy cones after a summer downpour will pull the branches down. If it flops, cut them for the vase.
seasonNotes.8: The white is ageing to pink. That's the plant doing what it should, not fading.

plants.name: Pickerelweed
plants.guide: A native emergent marginal aquatic with glossy heart-shaped leaves and violet-blue flower spikes through summer — one of the best-behaved, most pollinator-friendly plants for a pond edge. It grows in a few inches of standing water at the shallow margin and spreads by rhizome into a soft colony.
plants.soilNotes: Marginal aquatic: plant in heavy loam or aquatic soil in a few inches of standing water at the pond edge. Not fussy about pH. Contain the pot or the rhizome if you don't want it to march along the whole margin.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to part sun — more sun means more flowers.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to about Zone 3; dies back to the rhizome each winter and returns in spring. No cold concern here.

propagate.description: Divide the rhizome in spring.

fertilize.description: Pond/bog plants in a living pond generally need no feeding — the water carries nutrients.

plants.name: Cardinal Flower
plants.guide: A native wet-margin perennial found growing on the property, kept as a pond-bog plant. Its late-summer spikes of intense scarlet are a hummingbird magnet — one of the few reds a ruby-throat can't resist. It wants consistently moist, rich soil at the water's edge and is short-lived unless it's allowed to self-sow.
plants.soilNotes: Rich, consistently moist to wet soil at the pond margin — it will not tolerate drying out. Slightly acidic to neutral. A mulch of leaf litter keeps the roots cool and damp.
plants.aspectPreference: Part shade to full sun as long as the soil stays wet; afternoon shade helps in the open.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to about Zone 3. Forms an overwintering basal rosette; keep it from being buried in wet leaves that can rot the crown. No cold concern here.

plants.name: Cattail
plants.guide: The classic brown-spike marsh plant, collected roadside and introduced to the pond. Handsome and good habitat — but an AGGRESSIVE colonizer by thick rhizome that can take over a pond margin and choke open water within a few seasons. This one is on the watch-list: enjoy it, but keep it contained.
plants.soilNotes: Grows in mud to a foot of standing water at the margin. Not fussy. The management issue is not the soil but the rhizome — a submerged barrier or a contained pocket is the only reliable way to hold it in one spot.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun.
plants.frostSensitivity: Fully hardy; dies back to the rhizome and returns each spring. No cold concern.

prune.description: Cut back old stalks in late fall or early spring; cutting below the waterline repeatedly is one way to weaken a colony you want to shrink.

propagate.description: Do NOT propagate — it spreads itself far too readily. The task is containment, not increase.

fertilize.description: Pond/bog plants in a living pond generally need no feeding — the water carries nutrients.

water.description: Lives in the pond — water level is the pond's job, not a watering task.

plants.name: Corkscrew Rush
plants.guide: An ornamental rush whose green stems curl and spiral like corkscrews — a textural novelty at the pond edge. A cultivar of the native soft rush, it wants wet feet at the shallow margin and stays a tidy clump rather than running.
plants.soilNotes: Wet, boggy soil or shallow standing water at the margin; tolerant of most pH. Keeps to a clump — well-behaved next to the cattail's aggression.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to part shade.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to about Zone 4; may look ragged over winter — cut back tired growth in spring. No cold concern here.

plants.name: Dwarf Papyrus
plants.guide: A compact papyrus with fine green pom-pom heads on slender stems — an architectural marginal for the pond edge. Smaller and better-mannered than true giant papyrus. It is the least cold-hardy of the pond plantings here, so overwintering is the open question.
plants.soilNotes: Wet soil or a few inches of standing water at the margin; rich medium. Not pH-fussy.

Treat it as an annual, OR lift it in fall and overwinter the pot indoors / in a frost-free spot. Worth deciding this fall (memory flags an overwinter question ~October).

plants.name: Bowles' Golden Sedge
plants.guide: A bright golden-yellow sedge that lights up a pond edge — arching grassy blades in near-fluorescent chartreuse, best colour in spring and early summer. A clumping sedge for wet margins, it brings the one colour (soft gold) the rest of the pond greens lack.
plants.soilNotes: Consistently moist to wet soil or the shallow margin; tolerant of most pH. Clumps rather than runs.
plants.aspectPreference: Part sun keeps the gold best; too much hot afternoon sun can scorch the fine blades, too much shade dulls the colour.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to about Zone 5; semi-evergreen, cut back tired foliage in spring. No cold concern here.

plants.name: Variegated Japanese Iris
plants.guide: The third of the pond irises (with the blue flag and yellow flag), and the showiest in leaf: its blades are striped green-and-cream and hold that variegation all season, unlike most variegated plants that green up in summer. Deep purple flowers with a small gold eye rise above the foliage in early-to-mid summer. A true Japanese water iris — it wants rich, acidic, wet soil while it's growing.
plants.soilNotes: Rich, moist-to-wet, ACIDIC soil at the pond margin — the acidic pond water suits it well (Japanese iris dislikes lime). One real care difference from the flag irises: Iris ensata wants abundant water spring through summer but prefers NOT to sit in deep standing water over winter — so a margin spot that's wet in the growing season and merely damp in winter is ideal, rather than fully submerged year-round. Worth checking how this one is actually sited.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to part shade; more sun means more flowers, but afternoon shade is fine at the pond edge.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to about Zone 4 — no cold concern at this elevation. Dies back to the rhizome in winter and returns in spring; leave a tidy cut-back for spring.

prune.description: Cut back spent bloom stalks after flowering; tidy winter-worn foliage in late fall or early spring.

propagate.description: Divide clumps in late summer, a few weeks after flowering, every 3–4 years to keep them vigorous.

fertilize.description: Japanese iris are hungry — a spring feed of an acidic (never lime) fertilizer or compost supports the big blooms.

water.description: Keep consistently wet through the growing season; do not let it dry out while budding and blooming.

repot.description: Not applicable — a pond-margin perennial, not a container plant.

inspect.description: Watch that it stays wet in the growing season; confirm it isn't sitting in deep water over winter (ensata dislikes that); watch for browse.

bloom.note: Deep purple flowers with a gold eye over striped leaves; local timing not yet observed.

plants.name: Pitcher Plant
plants.guide: A native carnivorous pitcher plant, grown here as a bog planting in the pond. Its upright hollow pitchers trap and digest insects — a striking, low-maintenance oddity for a sunny, permanently-wet, nutrient-poor pond margin. The exact species isn't pinned down (it is NOT the purple pitcher plant, Sarracenia purpurea — Paul ruled that out); which Sarracenia it is is an easy thing to settle on the ground when it pitchers and blooms.
plants.soilNotes: Wants a nutrient-POOR, acidic, permanently-wet bog — sphagnum/peat + sand, never garden soil or fertilizer (fertilizer kills Sarracenia). The pond margin's acidic water suits it; keep it out of any spot that collects leaf-litter mud or runoff, which would enrich the root zone it needs to stay lean.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun for the strongest pitchers and colour; tolerates part sun. An open pond-edge spot is ideal.
plants.frostSensitivity: Most native Sarracenia are very cold-hardy (well below this elevation) and go dormant in winter — leave the old pitchers until spring. The main overwinter concern is keeping the crown wet but not locked in solid ice for long stretches; a pond that doesn't freeze to the bottom is fine. (If the exact species turns out to be a tender one, revisit this.)

prune.description: In early spring, trim off winter-blackened pitchers before new growth pushes.

propagate.description: Divide the rhizome in early spring, or let it clump up.

fertilize.description: NEVER fertilize — it feeds on insects; fertilizer or rich soil is fatal.

water.description: Keep permanently wet with rainwater / pond water; never let the bog dry out.

repot.description: Not applicable — a pond-bog planting, not a container plant.

inspect.description: Keep the crown wet and the root zone low-nutrient; remove any leaf-mud smothering it. When it pitchers/blooms, note the species to settle the ID.

bloom.note: Sarracenia send up nodding flowers on tall stalks in spring; timing and flower colour here not yet observed (colour will also help ID the species).
