species.notes: Small lungless woodland salamanders in the Plethodon genus are typically the most abundant vertebrates on the forest floor at this elevation — easily outnumbering any mammal or bird. Entirely terrestrial; never enters water even to breed, laying eggs in moist soil or under logs. Most active in cool moist weather (spring and fall); retreats deep into soil during summer heat. Flip any log or flat rock in moist forest and one is likely underneath. The Blue Ridge / North GA Plethodon community includes several candidate species at this elevation — see taxonomic note below.
species.conservation: Genus-level common — Plethodon salamanders dominate Appalachian forest-floor biomass. Individual species status varies.

species.name: Slimy Salamander
species.habitat: Moist rocky slopes, ravines, cave entrances, and forest floor with deep leaf litter
species.appearance: Large black salamander with white or gold spots/flecks. Secretes a sticky mucus that is very difficult to wash off hands.
species.notes: Church Mountain Road's rocky wooded slopes are prime habitat. Similar lifestyle to the Red-backed Salamander but larger and prefers rockier terrain and steeper slopes. Named for the sticky mucus it produces as a defense — it will permanently stain clothing and takes repeated soap washings to remove from skin. Despite this, it's harmless. Found by flipping rocks and large logs in moist rocky areas, especially on north-facing slopes.

species.name: Two-lined Salamander (Eurycea sp.)
species.habitat: Under rocks in and alongside small, fast-moving streams — requires clean, cold, well-oxygenated water
species.appearance: Slender yellowish-green salamander with a dark stripe along each side. Bronze to yellow-orange back.
species.notes: The stream salamander. Where there's a healthy small stream at Church Mountain Road — Clear Creek and the seeps that feed it — there are Two-lined Salamanders under the rocks. Their presence is a bioindicator of excellent water quality — they're sensitive to sedimentation and pollution. Flip rocks in shallow stream margins to find them (replace rocks carefully — this is their home). Larvae live in streams for 1–3 years before metamorphosis. The first warm spring rains trigger breeding movements from stream edges.
species.conservation: Common in clean-water Blue Ridge streams — a good bioindicator of stream health

Jan.highlights: Deep winter — most amphibians dormant or inactive underground. Check under logs on mild days for Red-backed Salamanders.

Feb.highlights: FIRST CALLS. Spring Peepers begin calling on the first warm rainy night (above 45°F). Spotted Salamander breeding migration to pond on first warm rain. Watch Feb 20–28 closely.

Mar.highlights: Peak spring frog calling. Spotted Salamander eggs visible in pond. American Toad first calls. Upland Chorus Frog wrapping up season.

Apr.highlights: American Toad peak calling from pond margins. First Green Frogs active on pond edge. Gray Treefrogs calling on warm nights. Red-backed Salamanders very active.

May.highlights: Full pond chorus on warm nights. Bullfrog calling begins. Toad breeding at peak. All salamanders active in moist areas.

Jun.highlights: Bullfrog jug-o-rum dominant at night. Toadlets emerging from pond (hundreds of tiny toads at pond edge). Gray Treefrog calling before rain.

Jul.highlights: Peak summer pond activity. Bullfrog and Green Frog territorial males along pond margins. Gray Treefrog abundant. Salamanders retreat to cool soil in heat.

Aug.highlights: Late summer pond activity. Frog chorus diminishing but Bullfrogs active. Salamanders begin returning to surface activity as nights cool.

Sep.highlights: Marbled Salamander breeding migration to dry pond basins on warm nights Sep–Oct. All surface salamanders becoming more active as temperatures moderate.

Oct.highlights: Marbled Salamander peak breeding — females guarding eggs in dry leaf litter near pond. Salamanders very active on forest floor after rain.

Nov.highlights: Late activity before winter dormancy. Check pond edges for last Bullfrog sightings. Two-lined Salamanders active in stream even in cold water.

Dec.highlights: Nearly all frogs and toads dormant. Two-lined Salamanders remain active in cold streams year-round. Red-backed Salamanders active on mild days above 40°F.

_meta.habitatContext: Mountain property at 2,873 ft with a mix of mature deciduous forest, rocky slopes, a pond, seasonal seeps, and edge habitat where forest meets clearing. North Georgia's Blue Ridge supports roughly 30 snake species; this set is the dozen most likely to be encountered on or near the property. Two are venomous (copperhead, timber rattlesnake) — both are pit vipers with heat-sensing facial pits. The rest are entirely harmless and many are actively beneficial (rodent and slug control, copperhead predation).
_meta.notes: Snakes are most active April through October at this elevation; most brumate (winter dormancy, not true hibernation) November–March in burrows, root cavities, rock crevices, and old foundations. Activity is strongly temperature-driven — warm sunny days following rain are peak movement windows in spring and fall. Of Georgia's 46 native snake species, only 6 are venomous; copperhead is by far the most likely on this property, with timber rattlesnake possible but uncommon. The other 10 species here are harmless and ecologically important — kingsnakes in particular are immune to pit viper venom and actively prey on copperheads.

propertyHighlights.whatToExpect: The most-encountered snake on the property is likely the Eastern Garter Snake (around the pond, garden edges, woodpiles) followed by the Ring-necked Snake (under flat rocks and logs in moist forest). Eastern Rat Snakes are large and conspicuous — often seen climbing trees raiding bird nests or crossing the road on warm afternoons. Copperhead awareness matters most April–October in transition zones: leaf litter at forest edges, rock walls, woodpiles, and around outbuildings.
propertyHighlights.safetyNotes: If you find a venomous snake, give it space and walk around — bites almost always happen during handling attempts or accidental contact in unwatched footing. Wear closed shoes (not flip-flops) when walking through tall grass or moving wood/rocks. Use a flashlight at night around the pond and walkways April–October. In a snakebite emergency, call 911 and Georgia Poison Center (1-800-222-1222) — do NOT apply ice, tourniquet, or attempt suction. Keep the bitten limb still and at about heart level, and remove any rings or watches before swelling starts. Most US snakebite deaths are 1–6 per year out of 7,000–8,000 bites.

lookalikePairs.notes: Cottonmouth (Agkistrodon piscivorus) does NOT occur in Pickens County — its northern range edge in Georgia is well south of here. Any 'water moccasin' at this elevation is almost certainly a harmless Northern Water Snake.

lookalikePairs.pair: Eastern Rat Snake vs. Black Racer
lookalikePairs.notes: Both are large and mostly black. Rat Snake has a distinctly checkered belly and rectangular body cross-section; Racer has a plain belly and rounder body. Racers are notably faster.

Many harmless juvenile snakes have hourglass-like blotches and can be mistaken for copperheads. Copperhead crossbands are well-defined, narrower across the top of the back and widest on the sides ('Hershey's Kiss' shape), and the head is distinctly broad and triangular.

species.name: Copperhead
species.habitat: Mixed deciduous forest with leaf litter, rocky outcrops, stone walls, woodpiles, building foundations, forest edges near streams. Will use almost any habitat with cover and prey.
species.appearance: Stocky body with distinctive copper-tan or pinkish-brown ground color overlaid by dark crossbands shaped like Hershey's Kisses (narrow on the spine, wide on the sides). Triangular head wider than neck; vertical (cat-eye) pupils; heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril. Juveniles have bright sulphur-yellow tail tips used as a lure to attract small prey.
species.notes: The venomous snake to know on this property. Copperheads are common throughout the southern Appalachians and are responsible for the most snakebites in the US — though deaths are extraordinarily rare (the venom is hemotoxic and painful but generally not life-threatening to healthy adults; still requires immediate medical attention). Their leaf-litter camouflage is among the best of any North American snake — most bites happen when someone steps on or reaches near an unseen snake. They are ambush predators that will hold position rather than flee. Most active on warm humid evenings April through October; nocturnal in summer heat. Diet: rodents, frogs, lizards, large insects, cicadas (a major late-summer food). Give them space and walk around — they don't pursue.

species.name: Timber Rattlesnake
species.habitat: Mature mountain forests, rocky south-facing slopes (used as winter dens), stream corridors. Prefers undisturbed wooded terrain — encounters near houses are rare.
species.appearance: Heavy-bodied with two color phases — yellow (tan to brown with dark chevron crossbands) and black (very dark, often with rust dorsal stripe). Distinctive segmented rattle on tail tip (may be missing in young or injured snakes). Triangular head, vertical pupils, heat-sensing pits.
species.notes: Possible in the surrounding mature mountain forest, though far less commonly encountered than copperhead — and remarkably docile when seen. Most will rattle and hold ground rather than strike if given space. Despite the more potent venom, bites are very rare because the snake announces itself and avoids people. Timber rattlesnakes hibernate communally in traditional rocky den sites used for generations. Listed as a species of conservation concern in Georgia due to habitat loss and persecution. If you ever see one on the property, count yourself lucky — this is a rare and ecologically valuable predator. Same response as copperhead: back away, don't handle, and there's no reason to kill one — it will move on. (Note: Georgia's law protecting non-game snakes exempts venomous species, so the timber rattlesnake is not legally protected here — but the harmless snakes on this list, like the racer, kingsnake, ratsnake and watersnake, ARE protected by law.) Diet: rodents (a major check on rodent-borne disease).
species.conservation: Not state-listed in Georgia (venomous species are exempt from the non-game protection law); declining range-wide from habitat loss and persecution

species.name: Eastern Rat Snake
species.habitat: Forests, forest edges, barns and outbuildings, stone walls, around houses. Excellent climber — often found in trees, on roofs, in rafters.
species.appearance: Adults shiny black above, often retaining faint remnants of juvenile blotching. Belly distinctly checkered (white with black squares — the field mark separating it from the Black Racer's plain belly). Body cross-section is squared off ('loaf of bread' shape) rather than round. Juveniles look very different — gray with bold dark blotches; commonly mistaken for copperheads but lack the triangular head and pit-viper features.
species.notes: The largest snake at Church Mountain Road and one of the most beneficial — a single adult eats dozens of rodents per year. Climbs trees to raid bird nests for eggs and nestlings (a natural part of forest dynamics, though notable for bluebird/box-nester monitoring). When cornered, vibrates tail in dry leaves to mimic a rattlesnake. Sometimes called 'black rat snake' under the older taxonomy (Elaphe obsoleta). If you find one in an outbuilding, the only good response is to leave it alone — the rodents it eats would otherwise eat your seed, wiring, and insulation.

species.name: Eastern Garter Snake
species.habitat: Almost anywhere with cover and moisture — pond edges, garden borders, woodpiles, grassy openings, stone walls, garages. Probably the most encountered snake on the property.
species.appearance: Slender. Three yellow longitudinal stripes (one mid-back, one on each side low on the body) against a dark olive or brown background. Checkered pattern between the stripes. Distinctive yellow chin and pale belly.
species.notes: Active in cooler weather than most snakes — often the first snake seen in late winter and the last in late fall. Cold-tolerant due to its northern range. Releases a strong musky smell from cloacal glands when handled (harmless but memorable). Bears live young (no eggs) in late summer — sometimes 20+ tiny garter snakes appear in late August. Diet: earthworms, slugs, frogs, small fish, salamanders. Mildly venomous saliva immobilizes prey but is completely harmless to humans.

species.name: Northern Water Snake
species.habitat: Pond margins, lake edges, slow streams, beaver impoundments. Often seen basking on rocks, logs, or overhanging branches at the water's edge; quickly dives in if approached.
species.appearance: Stout-bodied. Dark brown to gray with darker squarish crossbands on the neck transitioning to alternating side blotches farther down the body. Older individuals often appear nearly uniform dark from a distance. Belly white to yellow with reddish-orange half-moons. Rounded pupils.
species.notes: The pond snake. Frequently misidentified as a cottonmouth ('water moccasin') and killed unjustly — but the cottonmouth's northernmost Georgia range is well south of Pickens County, so any water snake at this elevation is harmless. Bold and defensive when cornered; will bite repeatedly and emits strong musk, but is not venomous. Diet is almost entirely fish and frogs — a sign of a healthy pond food web. Bears live young in late summer.

species.name: Ring-necked Snake
species.habitat: Moist deciduous forest floor under flat rocks, logs, bark slabs, leaf litter. Common around stone walls and old foundations. Almost never seen above ground in the open.
species.appearance: Small and slender. Uniform slate gray, olive, or black above with a vivid yellow or yellow-orange ring around the neck — unmistakable. Belly is brilliant yellow-orange, often with a row of small dark spots. Underside of tail tip especially bright.
species.notes: One of the most common but rarely seen snakes at Church Mountain Road — flip enough flat rocks or rotting logs in moist forest and you'll find them. When threatened, coils the tail tightly to display the bright belly as a warning flash. Diet: small salamanders, earthworms, slugs, juvenile lizards. Mildly venomous saliva (rear-fanged) immobilizes invertebrate prey — completely harmless to humans; even repeated bite attempts can't break skin. Lays small clutches of eggs (3–10) in moist soil June–July.

species.name: Eastern Kingsnake
species.habitat: Forest edges, fields, swamp margins, around farms and outbuildings. Often found near streams and pond edges.
species.appearance: Glossy black with a thin yellowish-white chain-link pattern — pale bands that fork and connect across the back creating a chain or speckled appearance. Belly checkered black-and-white.
species.notes: Famous for eating other snakes — including copperheads, to whose venom they are immune. A resident kingsnake is the best natural copperhead control available. Also eats rodents, lizards, birds, eggs. Constrictor (not venomous). Sometimes confused with the much smaller Scarlet Kingsnake (mountain-rare), Black Racer (no chain pattern), or Eastern Rat Snake (no chain pattern, has checkered belly). When threatened, vibrates tail and may release musk. Generally a calm, slow-moving snake compared to racers.
species.conservation: Populations have declined in parts of the southeast; mountain populations appear stable

species.name: Black Racer
species.habitat: Open woods, fields, forest edges, brushy areas, around barns. Prefers warmer, more open habitat than the Eastern Rat Snake.
species.appearance: Slender, uniformly satin black above with a white chin and throat (often extending onto the belly's first third). Belly mostly plain gray-black — no checkering (the key separator from Eastern Rat Snake). Large eyes for an active visual hunter. Juveniles look entirely different — gray with dark blotches that fade with age.
species.notes: Lives up to the name — among the fastest snakes in North America and an active diurnal hunter that chases down prey rather than ambushing. Will climb shrubs and low trees but is mostly terrestrial. Despite the species name 'constrictor', it doesn't actually constrict — it pins prey with body coils and swallows it alive. Will bite repeatedly if cornered (and most do not back down) but is harmless. Often seen crossing roads or basking on warm pavement on sunny mornings.

species.name: Rough Green Snake
species.habitat: Shrubs, vines, low tree branches especially near water and forest edges. Often around blackberry thickets, pond-edge willows, mountain laurel. Camouflages perfectly against green foliage.
species.appearance: Slender, bright leaf-green above, yellow-white below. Scales are keeled (rough texture, hence 'rough' green). Turns dull blue-gray after death — preserved specimens look nothing like living animals.
species.notes: One of the most beautiful and gentle snakes anywhere — virtually never bites, slow-moving by nature. Spends its life climbing slowly through low vegetation hunting insects, spiders, and tree frogs. Easy to overlook because of perfect camouflage. Active during the day. Lays small clutches of eggs in rotting wood or leaf litter. Sensitive to pesticides because it concentrates them by eating insects — its presence would indicate a pesticide-light area. Plausible at the property in pond-edge willows, mountain laurel, and forest-edge briars, though the camouflage means it could easily be present and unseen.
species.conservation: Common but declining in agricultural regions due to pesticide use

species.name: Eastern Hognose Snake
species.habitat: Sandy and loamy soils, old fields, forest edges, garden areas — anywhere with toads and diggable soil. Less common in heavy clay or pure forest interior.
species.appearance: Stout, with a distinctive upturned (hog-like) snout used for digging up toads. Highly variable color: brown, gray, yellow, orange, or solid black 'melanistic' phase, often with dark blotches. When threatened, flattens neck into a cobra-like hood and hisses loudly. If hissing doesn't work, rolls onto its back, mouth agape, tongue lolling, and plays dead (will flip itself back over if righted — comedic and unmistakable).
species.notes: A theatrical snake worth watching for, though habitat fit is borderline at the property — Hognose prefer sandy and loamy soils with abundant toads, and the property's clay-rich mountain forest sits at the edge of typical habitat. If one does show up: the bluff display — hooding, hissing, mock-striking with the mouth closed — is so dramatic many people assume it's deadly. It is entirely harmless: even when frightened it almost never bites, and its mild rear-fanged saliva is toad-specific (it's immune to toad parotoid gland toxins). Diet is almost entirely toads. Worth watching for in spring near the pond and along sandy/disturbed edges (gravel drives) when toads are breeding.
species.conservation: Common but declining in some areas

species.name: Dekay's Brown Snake
species.habitat: Under leaf litter, flowerpots, mulch, boards, flat rocks, garden edges. Highly tolerant of human activity — common in suburbs and around houses.
species.appearance: Small, slender. Brown to gray-brown above with a paler stripe down the spine bordered by two parallel rows of small dark spots. Belly pinkish-white. Often mistaken for a large worm or a baby of a larger snake species.
species.notes: Probably present in greater numbers than you'd expect — they're cryptic and rarely seen except when you flip a board or pot in the garden. Diet is almost entirely slugs and earthworms, making them one of the best garden allies. Extremely docile — virtually never bites; the mouth is too small to do anything anyway. Bears live young in late summer. Often turns up in basements and crawl spaces after heavy rain — relocate gently to a mulched garden bed.

species.name: Worm Snake
species.habitat: Burrows in moist forest soil, under rocks and rotting logs, leaf litter. Rarely active above ground except during rainy spring nights.
species.appearance: Tiny and looks remarkably like a large earthworm — uniform glossy pink-brown above, pink belly. Pointed head with a spine-like tail tip used to anchor while burrowing. Smooth, shiny scales.
species.notes: The most worm-like snake imaginable. Spends nearly all its time underground hunting earthworms (its sole food). The pointed tail tip is sometimes pressed against a handler's skin in a brief poke — harmless and often mistaken for a sting. Completely docile, won't bite. Likely present somewhere in the property's moist forest soil — they're cryptic enough that absence-of-sighting doesn't mean absence-of-presence. Most often turned up by gardeners digging in moist soil or by overturning old logs. A sign of healthy soil with abundant earthworms.
species.conservation: Common but rarely observed due to fossorial lifestyle

Jan.highlights: All snakes brumating underground or in rocky dens. Watch for early-season movement on unusually warm February days following warm rains.

Feb.highlights: Garter snakes may emerge briefly on warm sunny afternoons. All venomous species remain dormant.

Mar.highlights: First emergence. Garter snakes around pond and garden edges on warm days. Rat snakes emerging from foundations and rock walls late in month.

Apr.highlights: Spring emergence in full swing. First copperhead sightings — watch footing in leaf litter and around rock walls. Northern Water Snakes basking at pond edge. Mating season for several species.

May.highlights: Peak diversity. All species active. Hognose snakes hunting breeding toads at the pond. Rough Green Snakes in pond-edge shrubs. Kingsnakes patrolling for other snakes — leave them alone.

Jun.highlights: Active month. Rat snakes raiding bird nests. Egg-laying for most oviparous species. Use a flashlight on walkways at dusk.

Jul.highlights: Summer heat — most snakes nocturnal or crepuscular. Daytime activity reduced; check sheltered spots (under boards, foundation cracks).

Aug.highlights: Live-bearing species (garter, water snakes) give birth — small juveniles appearing. Cicada emergence draws copperheads to oak woodlands at night.

Sep.highlights: Second peak of the year. Cooler nights push reptiles back to daytime activity. Copperheads especially active hunting toward winter den sites.

Oct.highlights: Fall migration to denning sites. Garter snakes congregate near hibernacula. Last warm days for copperhead encounters.

Nov.highlights: Most snakes have entered brumation. Garter snakes may still emerge briefly on warm afternoons.

Dec.highlights: All snakes dormant in dens, root cavities, foundations, and rock crevices. Resume watching late February.

_meta.habitatContext: North Georgia is at the northern range edge for several southern lizards and the southern edge for a few northern species, producing modest lizard diversity at 2,873 ft. The property's mix of sun-warmed rock walls, fallen logs, wood piles, leaf litter, and forest edges supports a small but rewarding cast of native lizards. None are venomous and all are harmless. Skinks are the dominant family — fast, glossy, often blue-tailed as juveniles.
_meta.notes: All native eastern US lizards are harmless. The 'blue-tailed' lizards Paul has seen are almost certainly juvenile Five-lined or Broad-headed Skinks — both species sport vivid blue tails as juveniles and lose the color with maturity. Lizards are diurnal and strongly tied to sun and warm surfaces, so peak activity is mid-morning to mid-afternoon April through September. Most retreat to leaf litter, rotting logs, or rock crevices by October and remain dormant through winter.

propertyHighlights.whatToExpect: Five-lined Skinks are the most commonly seen lizard — basking on log piles, stone walls, and the sunny side of outbuildings. Eastern Fence Lizards prefer rough vertical surfaces (the namesake fence posts, dead-standing pines, granite outcrops). Ground Skinks are easy to miss because they slip through leaf litter looking like tiny snakes. Broad-headed Skinks (much larger) are more arboreal and often spotted in oak trees. Six-lined Racerunners need open sun-baked sand or gravel and are at the property's elevation limit — possible but not guaranteed.
propertyHighlights.blueTailedNote: Paul's 'blue-tailed skink' is the juvenile of either the Five-lined Skink (most likely — common, widespread) or the larger Broad-headed Skink. Both species have brilliant electric-blue tails as juveniles that fade to gray-brown as they mature. The blue color is thought to draw predator attacks toward the detachable tail rather than the head — a survival trade-off where the lizard escapes with a stub and regrows a duller replacement.
identificationTips: If it's tiny, slim, and moves through leaf litter like a worm with legs — Ground Skink.
If it has a wedge-shaped head and rough spiny scales, often on bark or fence rails — Eastern Fence Lizard (males flash iridescent blue belly patches in spring).
If it's glossy with stripes and a blue tail (juvenile) or a uniform brown-bronze body (adult), 4–8 inches — Five-lined Skink.
Same pattern as Five-lined but noticeably larger and often high in a tree, with an orange-red head on adult males — Broad-headed Skink.
If it has bright yellow longitudinal stripes on dark background and runs astonishingly fast in open sandy areas — Six-lined Racerunner (uncommon at this elevation).

species.name: Five-lined Skink
species.habitat: Logs, stumps, wood piles, rock walls, foundations, mulched garden edges. Anywhere with cover near sun.
species.appearance: Juveniles: glossy black with five cream-yellow longitudinal stripes and an unmistakable bright electric-blue tail. Adult females: stripes fade to bronze, tail goes blue-gray. Adult males: stripes nearly invisible, body turns olive-brown, and the head flushes orange-red during spring breeding season. Smooth shiny scales (skinks look 'polished' compared to fence lizards).
species.notes: The classic 'blue-tailed skink' of southern yards. Extremely fast — usually spotted as a streak across a log followed by stillness against tree bark. The blue tail is detachable: if a predator grabs it, the tail breaks off and wriggles violently while the lizard escapes; a duller replacement regrows over weeks but never matches the original. Females coil around their eggs in rotting logs and defend them against beetles and ants — unusual maternal behavior for a lizard. Diet: insects, spiders, small invertebrates. Will bite if handled but the jaws can't break adult human skin.

species.name: Broad-headed Skink
species.habitat: Mature oak and other hardwood trees, especially with hollow cavities or dead standing wood. Will use the same cover as Five-lined Skink but climbs much more.
species.appearance: Same general body pattern as Five-lined Skink but substantially larger. Juveniles have the same blue tail. Adult males develop a dramatically broad, swollen orange-red head during breeding season (April–June) — looks almost like a different species. Females retain faded stripes throughout life. Best distinguished from Five-lined Skink by size (much larger) and scale-count details around the lip (5 supralabial scales before the eye vs. 4 in Five-lined).
species.notes: The big skink of mature oak forests. Often spotted high in trees rather than on the ground. Males in breeding condition with their swollen orange heads are unmistakable. Important predator of cicadas, large beetles, and spiders. Will bite hard if handled — the jaws are strong enough to draw blood from an adult. Found around rotting hardwood snags and tree cavities; old hollow oaks at Church Mountain Road are prime habitat.
species.conservation: Common but less abundant than Five-lined

species.name: Eastern Fence Lizard
species.habitat: Fence posts, wood piles, dead standing pines, granite outcrops, sunny edges of mixed pine-hardwood forest. Prefers vertical rough surfaces for basking and quick escape.
species.appearance: Gray to brown with wavy dark crossbands on the back. Strongly keeled (spiny) scales give a rough sandpapery look — unlike the smooth gloss of skinks. Males have iridescent blue patches on the throat and along the belly, edged with black; visible when the lizard does 'push-up' territorial displays from a fence post or log. Females duller, often greenish with subtle barring.
species.notes: The 'push-up lizard.' Males do conspicuous head-bobs and push-ups from prominent perches to defend territory — a charming and watchable behavior in spring. When approached, freezes against bark trusting camouflage; if pushed, sprints around the back side of the trunk. More cold-tolerant than other Georgia lizards — active earlier in spring and later into fall. Diet: insects and spiders. Studies in fire ant zones show fence lizards in the southeast have evolved longer legs as an escape adaptation — a real-time evolution story.

species.name: Ground Skink
species.habitat: Leaf litter on the forest floor, under fallen bark, around stumps, in moist mulched beds. Almost never climbs.
species.appearance: Tiny and slender. Coppery-brown to bronze above with a clean dark brown stripe along each side from snout through eye to tail. Belly white or yellow. Looks more like a small snake than a typical lizard because the legs are very short relative to body length.
species.notes: One of the smallest lizards in North America and easy to mistake for a snake when it slips through leaf litter. Lives essentially its entire life in the top inch of forest floor litter. Diet: small insects, spider, springtails, mites. Detachable tail (regrows shorter). Lays 1–7 tiny eggs in soil under cover objects. Probably much more abundant on the property than sightings would suggest — flip enough damp leaf piles and bark slabs and you'll find them.

species.name: Six-lined Racerunner
species.habitat: Open sunny sandy or rocky areas with sparse vegetation — roadside cuts, gravel drives, granite outcrops, old fields. Avoids dense forest.
species.appearance: Slender with a very long tail (most of total length). Dark brown to black background with six bright yellow-green longitudinal stripes from neck to tail. Belly white in females, often pale blue-green in males. Males may show throat color in summer.
species.notes: Among the fastest lizards in North America — can hit nearly 18 mph in short bursts. Active only on the hottest sunny days; retreats to burrows by mid-afternoon if cloudy. At 2,873 ft the property is at or above this species' typical elevation limit in Georgia — Racerunners are far more common in the Piedmont and on warm low-elevation south-facing slopes. Possible in disturbed sunny edges (gravel drives, granite outcrops) but well outside guaranteed habitat. If you ever spot one here, it'll be both the fastest small thing you've seen all year and a noteworthy elevation record.
species.conservation: Common range-wide; locally limited by habitat at this elevation

Jan.highlights: All lizards dormant in soil, leaf litter, or rock crevices.

Feb.highlights: Still dormant. First emergence usually waits for sustained warm afternoons in mid-March.

Mar.highlights: First emergence on warm sunny days. Fence Lizards earliest — already basking on south-facing surfaces.

Apr.highlights: Spring emergence in full swing. Male skinks beginning to flush orange-red. Fence lizard territorial push-up displays.

May.highlights: Peak breeding. Male skinks brilliantly colored. Egg-laying begins late month. Watch log piles and rock walls for displaying males.

Jun.highlights: Females guarding nests in rotting logs and soil. All species active. Hottest direct-sun perches occupied throughout midday.

Jul.highlights: Hatchlings emerging — first appearance of new generation blue-tailed juvenile skinks late month.

Aug.highlights: Juvenile skinks abundant — peak month for spotting electric-blue tails. Watch around log piles and stone walls.

Sep.highlights: Cooler nights — lizards basking longer in morning sun. Last activity month for racerunners.

Oct.highlights: Fall retreat to overwintering cover. Fence lizards latest active. By month end most have settled into leaf litter or root cavities.

Dec.highlights: Dormant. Look for them again in mid-to-late March.

_meta.habitatContext: The singing insects are the property's loudest wildlife and its least documented. Mature oak-hickory canopy supplies the cicadas and true katydids; the clearing edge, mulched beds and pond margin supply the crickets and bush katydids; and the leaf litter supplies the ground crickets that sit under everything else. Elevation matters more here than for any other domain on the property — 2,873 ft is cool enough to plausibly hold a northern cicada that never reaches Atlanta, and cool enough that the autumn chorus shuts down earlier in the evening than it does downhill.
_meta.notes: ⚠️ NO SPECIES IN THIS FILE HAS BEEN CONFIRMED AT THE PROPERTY. Every record here is a range-and-habitat inference — the species is documented in the north Georgia Blue Ridge and the property has the habitat it wants. That is why every record carries `presence.confidence: inferred` and `presence.askable: true`. This is the only domain in the record that is honest-uncertain from top to bottom, and a single evening on the porch with the app open can start settling it. Timing is temperature-driven and shifts a week or more year to year; at 2,873 ft expect the chorus to start later in summer and quit earlier in autumn than lowland north Georgia.

propertyHighlights.whyItSounds: Church Mountain Road has the two things a loud summer night needs: unbroken hardwood canopy and a warm open edge. True katydids and cicadas sing from the tops of the oaks and hickories — you almost never see them, you only ever hear them. The open clearing, the mulched beds and the pond margin give the crickets and the smaller bush katydids their low, close-in layer. The result is a chorus with real vertical structure: the cicadas overhead by day, the katydids overhead by night, and the crickets down at ankle height around the house from dusk until the cold shuts them off.
howToListen: Height tells you the family. Overhead in the canopy = cicada (day) or true katydid (night). Chest height in a shrub = bush katydid or jumping bush cricket. At your feet in the leaves = ground cricket.

Time of day is the strongest single filter. Cicadas are the daytime sound and go quiet at dark; katydids and most crickets don't start until dusk. Nothing at Fernwood sings loudly in both halves of the day except the trigs.

Rhythm separates the cicadas. A steady unbroken buzz is a Lyric Cicada; a rattling pulse like a shaken salt shaker is Linne's; a slow build to a crescendo and an abrupt stop is the Morning Cicada, and it will be before noon.
Temperature sets the tempo. The same katydid sings fast and frantic at 84°F and slow and draggy at 58°F — it is the same species, running at a different speed.

keyEvents.name: The chorus starts
keyEvents.description: The first cicadas start in the canopy in late June, and the first true katydid usually follows in the first days of July. Before that the summer nights here are close to silent.
keyEvents.elevation_note: At 2,873 ft this runs perhaps a week behind lowland north Georgia — the exact lag is unmeasured, and a first-katydid date logged here would be the first real number we have.

keyEvents.name: Peak — the wall of sound
keyEvents.description: Every species is out at once and the night chorus stops being individual insects and becomes one pulsing wall that seems to breathe. This is the loudest the property gets all year, louder than the spring peepers.
keyEvents.elevation_note: Overlaps almost exactly with the amphibian off-season, so August is the one month the night noise is entirely insect.

keyEvents.name: The handoff to crickets
keyEvents.description: The cicadas finish first and the days go quiet. Then the katydids thin out, and what is left after dark is the cricket layer — field crickets, ground crickets, tree crickets — quieter, lower and much more temperature-sensitive.
keyEvents.elevation_note: Cool nights arrive early up here, so the handoff should be noticeably earlier than in Jasper town.

keyEvents.name: Silence at 52°F
keyEvents.description: Common True Katydids stop singing altogether below about 52°F. On a clear autumn night the chorus does not fade gradually — it switches off as the temperature crosses that line, and the on-site station can watch it happen.
keyEvents.elevation_note: The property crosses 52°F on many October nights that stay above it 1,400 ft downhill, which is why autumn evenings here go quiet weeks before they do in town.

keyEvents.name: Brood XIX periodical cicadas
keyEvents.window: May–June of a brood year — last 2024, next 2037
keyEvents.description: Brood XIX, the Great Southern Brood, is Georgia's 13-year periodical cicada and the largest brood in North America. It last emerged in spring 2024 and is not due again until 2037. In a brood year the sound is nothing like the annual cicadas: it arrives in May rather than July, it is a continuous roar rather than individual singers, and it comes from red-eyed black cicadas you can see rather than the green ones you never do.
keyEvents.elevation_note: ⚠️ Whether Brood XIX actually reaches this ridge is UNVERIFIED. It is recorded across north Georgia and 75 counties reported it in 2011, but periodical emergences are notoriously patchy at the scale of a single hillside, and nobody has recorded whether Church Mountain Road was inside or outside it in 2024. Worth asking anyone who was here that May. (The 17-year Brood VI does NOT reach here — its only Georgia county is Rabun, three counties east.)

species.name: Common True Katydid
species.statusLabel: The sound of an August night
species.perch: High in the canopy of oaks, hickories and maples — 30 to 60 ft up
species.song: A harsh, rasping phrase of two to four pulses, repeated over and over from the treetops. In the Southeast the phrase runs faster and carries more pulses than the leisurely northern 'ka-ty-did'.
species.soundsLike: katy-DID, katy-DIDN'T — the insect the whole family is named for
species.chorusRole: The bass line. When hundreds call at once they fall in and out of sync and the whole hillside seems to pulse and breathe.
species.appearance: A big, deep-bodied, leaf-green katydid with strongly veined wings held tent-like over the body. Almost never seen — it stays high, it is the exact colour of a leaf, and it stops singing when you get close.
species.notes: This is the species people mean when they say 'the katydids are loud tonight'. It is also the best natural thermometer on the property after the tree crickets: the song rate tracks air temperature directly, so an 84°F night sounds frantic and a 58°F night sounds like the same insect running at half speed. Below about 52°F it stops entirely — on a cooling October night the chorus does not fade, it switches off. Because it sings from the canopy and never comes down, the odds of ever seeing one here are low; this is a species you will only ever know by ear.

presence.basis: Universal in mature eastern hardwood forest across its range, and the property is exactly that. Unconfirmed here only because nobody has written it down.

photos.author: Seth Shively
photos.place: Cotton Belt Trail, Waco, TX, US

photos.author: gbasstx
photos.place: N Frazier St, Conroe, TX, US

species.name: Snowy Tree Cricket
species.perch: Shrubs, brambles and the low branches of small trees, usually 3–10 ft up
species.song: Pure, mellow, evenly spaced whistled notes — 'treet ... treet ... treet' — with a soft bell-like quality nothing else here matches. Every snowy within earshot synchronizes, so a whole hillside pulses together in perfect time.
species.soundsLike: a slow, sweet, unhurried whistle — the sound most people picture when they imagine a summer night
species.chorusRole: The metronome. Its pace is the most reliable temperature reading in the chorus.
species.appearance: A slender, delicate, very pale green cricket with broad flat wings held out over the back like a leaf. Far more often heard than seen despite singing at eye level.
species.notes: Count the chirps in 13 seconds, add 40, and you have the air temperature in °F. That is not a folk saying that mostly works — it is a calibrated relationship for eastern populations, and it is the one piece of weather folklore on this property that the on-site station can check directly. The synchrony is the other remarkable thing: the crickets are not following a leader, each one is adjusting to its neighbours, and the result is a hillside chirping in unison. If the whistle sounds rough or pulsing rather than clean and bell-like, you are hearing a different tree cricket and the formula will not hold.

presence.basis: Widespread across the eastern US including the southern Appalachians, and the shrubby clearing edge is good habitat. Unconfirmed here.

species.name: Lyric Cicada
species.perch: Trunks and high limbs of oaks and hickories
species.song: A steady, buzzy, rattling trill that runs unbroken for thirty seconds to a minute or more, with no rise and fall and no pulsing.
species.soundsLike: a long unbroken rattle — the one cicada that never seems to pause for breath
species.chorusRole: The easiest cicada here to name, precisely because it does NOT pulse. If the sound rattles evenly and just keeps going, it is this one.
species.appearance: Stout, green-and-black with dark wing veins and a distinctly reddish-brown cast to the underside. Like all annual cicadas, most often met as a discarded nymphal shell on a tree trunk.
species.notes: An oak-hickory forest specialist, which makes Church Mountain Road close to ideal for it. It sings through warm days but tends to peak at dusk, so it is often the last daytime sound before the katydids take over — the actual moment of handoff between the day chorus and the night one.

presence.basis: Documented across north Georgia in exactly this forest type. Unconfirmed here.

photos.author: mangumcl
photos.place: N Ninth St, De Queen, AR, US

species.name: Linne's Cicada
species.song: Begins softly, builds quickly, then settles into a rapid pulsating rattle before ending abruptly. About fifteen seconds start to finish.
species.soundsLike: a shaken salt shaker that speeds up, holds, and stops dead
species.chorusRole: The pulsing one. Where the Lyric Cicada is a flat rattle, this has an obvious rhythmic wobble in it.
species.appearance: Green and black with pale collar markings; wings clear with green veins.
species.notes: Sings through the whole warm part of the day, so on a hot July afternoon this and the Lyric are what you are hearing overhead. The abrupt ending is the giveaway — the song does not trail off, it stops as if switched off.

presence.basis: One of the commonest annual cicadas in north Georgia. Unconfirmed here.

species.name: Morning Cicada
species.perch: Trees near water — the pond margin is the likeliest spot here
species.song: A soft buzz that grows into a pulsating drone, swells to a crescendo, then tapers and stops abruptly. Ten to fifteen seconds.
species.soundsLike: a wave building and breaking — and almost always before noon
species.chorusRole: The clock. If a cicada is singing hard at eight in the morning and quiet by two in the afternoon, this is the one.
species.appearance: Black with green markings and a distinct white or pale patch on each side of the thorax.
species.notes: Also catalogued as the Swamp Cicada, and the two names capture the two things worth knowing about it: it likes low wet ground, and it sings in the morning rather than the afternoon. The morning habit is unusual enough to be a reliable field mark on its own. Its taste for wet lowland is also why it is the least likely of the four annual cicadas here — the pond helps its case, but 2,873 ft is above where this species usually lives.
species.conservation: Common at lower elevations across the Southeast

presence.basis: Common in lowland Georgia and associated with wet ground; the property has a pond but sits well above its usual elevation band. Genuinely uncertain — a morning-singing cicada heard here would be worth reporting.

photos.author: richard crook
photos.place: 10216 Lee Rd, Boynton Beach, FL 33472, USA

photos.author: Brett Jackson
photos.place: Timber Cove, Taylor Lake Village, TX 77586, USA

species.name: Dog-day Cicada
species.song: A long, even, high-pitched buzz that swells slightly and fades, without the rattling pulse of the other cicadas here. Ten to twenty seconds.
species.soundsLike: a distant circular saw, or a power line humming on a hot afternoon
species.chorusRole: The smooth one. No rattle, no pulse — just a clean rising and falling whine.
species.appearance: Smaller and greener than the other annual cicadas here, with a frosted white bloom on the underside.
species.notes: ⭐ The most interesting record in this file and the least certain. This is a northern cicada — its range covers the upper Midwest, New England and Canada, and it reaches the South only by climbing: it follows the Appalachians down as a cool-elevation relict, hanging on at heights that feel like New England to an insect. At 2,873 ft Fernwood is exactly the kind of place it could be, and it would never be found in Jasper town 1,400 ft below. Confirming a Dog-day Cicada here would be a genuine elevation record for the property and the single most valuable thing anyone could settle in this domain.
species.conservation: Common northward; local and elevation-restricted in the southern Appalachians

presence.basis: Southern range limit is elevation-dependent in the Appalachians and 2,873 ft is plausible, but there is no Pickens County record in hand. The highest-value unknown in this file.

species.name: Greater Anglewing
species.song: Two quite different songs: a loud, high, isolated 'tsip!' delivered every few seconds, and a rapid mechanical ticking — 'tick-tick-tick-tick' — like a tiny wind-up toy.
species.soundsLike: a single sharp lisp out of the dark, then later a rattling tick — frequently mistaken for a bird or a tree frog
species.chorusRole: The punctuation. Single notes that stand out cleanly against the katydid wall.
species.appearance: A large, beautifully leaf-shaped bright green katydid with a sharply angled wing edge — one of the best leaf mimics on the property.
species.notes: The isolated 'tsip' is one of the most commonly misidentified sounds of a southern summer night; people reliably report it as a bird. It is worth learning because once you can pick it out of the true katydid chorus you start hearing it everywhere. Attracted to porch lights, which makes this one of the few canopy katydids anyone actually gets a look at.

presence.basis: Widespread in Georgia in wooded and edge habitat. Unconfirmed here.

photos.author: pkryan33
photos.place: Tremont Rd, Pine Grove, PA, US

photos.author: Ethan Dropkin
photos.place: Liberty State Park, Jersey City, NJ, US

species.name: Lesser Anglewing
species.song: A short, coarse, raspy buzz — 'zeep ... zeep' — repeated at irregular intervals, rougher and less clean than the Greater Anglewing's sharp tick.
species.soundsLike: a brief scratchy rasp, like a zipper pulled two inches
species.chorusRole: The early bird. Often singing weeks before the true katydids get going.
species.appearance: Like a smaller Greater Anglewing — bright leaf-green, angled wings, superb camouflage.
species.notes: Worth knowing mainly for its timing: it starts well ahead of the Common True Katydid, so a raspy buzz from the trees in June, before the summer chorus proper has begun, is most likely this. By the time August arrives it is buried under everything else.

presence.basis: Common across Georgia in deciduous woodland edge. Unconfirmed here.

photos.author: Stott Noble
photos.place: Ruffner Mountain Nature Preserve, Birmingham, Alabama

photos.author: nje171
photos.place: Beaver Lake Dr, Ellijay, GA, US

species.name: Oblong-winged Katydid
species.perch: Shrubs, brambles and low trees along the clearing edge
species.song: A dry, two-parted phrase — 'tzeet-tzeet' — delivered every few seconds from low cover.
species.soundsLike: two short dry scrapes, close together, then a pause
species.chorusRole: Mid-height. Between the ground crickets and the canopy katydids.
species.appearance: Rounded, broad, leaf-green wings — noticeably less angular than the anglewings.
species.notes: Famous for a rare pink colour morph: perhaps one individual in several hundred hatches bright rose-pink instead of green, the result of a single recessive trait. Pink ones are conspicuous to predators and rarely survive long in the wild, which is why almost every photograph of one is from captivity. If a pink katydid ever turns up in the beds here, that is a genuinely remarkable find and worth photographing immediately.

presence.basis: Widespread in Georgia; the clearing edge and mulched beds are good habitat. Unconfirmed here.

photos.author: Tom Preney
photos.place: 5200 Matchette Rd, Windsor, ON N9C 4E8, Canada

species.name: Fork-tailed Bush Katydid
species.statusLabel: The one closest to the house
species.perch: Garden shrubs, ornamental beds, low foliage — routinely within a few feet of a door
species.song: A soft, lisping 'zeep', given as single notes at long and irregular intervals. Quiet enough to miss entirely unless the night is still.
species.soundsLike: a faint short lisp, minutes apart — the sound you notice only after you stop looking for it
species.chorusRole: The near one. Almost everything else in this file is singing from far away; this one is usually close enough to find with a flashlight.
species.appearance: Slender, bright green, with long delicate wings. Males have a small forked appendage at the tail end that gives the species its name.
species.notes: By far the most likely katydid to actually be seen at Fernwood rather than only heard, because it lives at eye level in exactly the planted beds people walk past. It also turns up on porch screens at night. If anyone wants to put a face to the summer chorus, this is the realistic candidate — track a 'zeep' with a flashlight and it will be sitting on a hydrangea leaf.

presence.basis: One of the commonest katydids in eastern North America and a habitual garden species. Unconfirmed here only for lack of a written record.

species.name: Sword-bearing Conehead
species.perch: Tall grass and weedy margins along the clearing edge
species.song: A long, relentless, mechanical series of quick rasps — 'tsip-tsip-tsip-tsip' — running on without variation for minutes at a time.
species.soundsLike: a lawn sprinkler ticking round, or an old sewing machine
species.chorusRole: The machine. Utterly regular, and once you hear it you cannot un-hear it.
species.appearance: Long, narrow, green or brown, with the pointed cone-shaped head the group is named for. Females carry a long straight ovipositor — the 'sword'.
species.notes: Coneheads live in grass rather than trees, so this one is tied to the open clearing edge rather than the forest. The song is so steady and so mechanical that people regularly mistake it for a piece of equipment left running somewhere down the hill. Coneheads can also give a painful nip if handled carelessly — they are strong-jawed for their size.
species.conservation: Common in grassland and old-field habitat

presence.basis: Widespread in the Southeast wherever there is tall grass; the clearing edge qualifies. Unconfirmed here.

photos.author: bertfoquet
photos.place: John T Mcnaughton Park, Pekin, IL, US

species.name: Fall Field Cricket
species.perch: Under stones, mulch, wood piles, doorsteps and foundation edges
species.song: The archetypal cricket chirp — short musical bursts at roughly two to three a second, from ground level.
species.soundsLike: 'cricket' — this is the sound the word means
species.chorusRole: The familiar one, and the one most likely to get indoors and sing from behind a baseboard.
species.appearance: Stout, glossy black, with long antennae and hind legs built for jumping.
species.notes: The autumn cricket. It gets going as the cicadas fade and is still singing after the katydids have quit, which makes it the last real voice of the season here — often the only thing audible on a still October evening. Cool nights slow it down noticeably before it stops for good.

presence.basis: Ubiquitous in eastern North America including the Blue Ridge. Unconfirmed here only for lack of a written record.

species.name: Carolina Ground Cricket
species.perch: Leaf litter, damp ground, the base of beds and the woodland floor
species.song: A soft, buzzy, uneven trill that swells and sags without ever quite stopping — pitched low and coming from everywhere at once.
species.soundsLike: a faint hiss under everything else, more texture than tune
species.chorusRole: The floor of the whole chorus. Almost nobody notices it until it is pointed out, and then it is impossible to ignore.
species.appearance: Tiny, dark brown, easily mistaken for a young field cricket. Runs rather than jumps when disturbed.
species.notes: This is the sound most people mentally file as 'quiet' on a late-summer evening. It is not quiet — it is thousands of very small crickets in the leaf litter, and it is arguably the single most abundant animal voice on the property. A good listening exercise: stand still at dusk in September and deliberately listen underneath the katydids.

presence.basis: One of the most abundant ground crickets in the eastern US, in exactly this leaf-litter habitat. Unconfirmed here only for lack of a written record.

species.name: Jumping Bush Cricket
species.perch: Shrubs and small trees, very often the ones planted right against a house
species.song: A single sharp, clean chirp, well separated — one every second or two — with a bright ringing quality.
species.soundsLike: a slow, deliberate 'chip ... chip ... chip', much more spaced out than a field cricket
species.chorusRole: The spacing is the tell. Same basic chirp as a field cricket, at a fraction of the speed and from up in a shrub rather than down on the ground.
species.appearance: Light brown, broad-winged, well camouflaged against bark.
species.notes: A strongly suburban-feeling cricket that likes ornamental plantings and building edges, so around the house it may well be the most audible cricket of late summer. Pairs naturally with the Fall Field Cricket as a listening exercise: same chirp, one fast and at your feet, one slow and above your head.

presence.basis: Common across Georgia in shrubby and planted habitat. Unconfirmed here.

species.name: Handsome Trig
species.perch: Low shrubs, vines, brambles and dense leafy growth
species.song: A rapid, buzzy, staccato phrase — 'chi-chi-chi-chi' — repeated in short bursts, surprisingly loud for the size of the insect.
species.soundsLike: a quick electric stutter from inside a bush
species.chorusRole: One of the very few things here that sings hard in broad daylight and after dark both.
species.appearance: Unmistakable and genuinely beautiful: a bright red-orange head and thorax, glossy black wings, and pale legs. Also catalogued as the Red-headed Bush Cricket.
species.notes: Worth seeking out on looks alone — it is one of the most striking insects on the property and quite unlike anything else in the record. Because it sings in daylight it is also the most findable: follow the stutter into a bramble patch on a July afternoon and there is a fair chance of actually seeing the singer, which is almost never true of anything else in this file.

presence.basis: Common across Georgia in dense low growth. Unconfirmed here.

photos.author: ltjeffers
photos.place: Shadow Creek Ranch, Pearland, TX, USA

species.name: Narrow-winged Tree Cricket
species.song: A rapid pulsing trill delivered in bursts — rougher, faster and less musical than the Snowy Tree Cricket's clean whistle.
species.soundsLike: a buzzy warble rather than a bell
species.chorusRole: The snowy's rougher cousin, and the main reason to listen carefully before trusting the cricket-thermometer count.
species.appearance: Slender and pale green like the Snowy Tree Cricket, but with narrower wings and a distinctly reddish or orange cast to the top of the head.
species.notes: Included mostly as a check on the thermometer trick. Both species are pale green tree crickets singing from foliage on the same summer nights, but only the Snowy's chirp rate maps onto temperature the way the folk formula says. If a count comes out badly wrong against the station reading, the likeliest explanation is that this is what was being counted.

presence.basis: Widespread in the eastern US in shrub and tree foliage. Unconfirmed here.

photos.author: Kyle Aldinger
photos.place: Zinn Chapel Rd, Reedsville, WV, US

photos.author: Sinéad Tuttle-Lerner
photos.place: South Branch Raritan River, Long Valley, NJ, US

Jan.highlights: Silent. The singing insects are overwintering as eggs in plant stems and soil, or as nymphs underground — the cicadas beneath the oaks are years into a multi-year development nobody can see.

Feb.highlights: Still silent. The first sound of the year at the property will be spring peepers at the pond, not insects — the insect chorus is more than four months away.

Mar.highlights: Nothing singing. Ground cricket and katydid eggs are beginning to develop as soil temperatures rise.

Apr.highlights: Nymphs hatching and growing, all of them mute — singing requires the adult wings, which are several moults away yet.

May.highlights: The very first voices. Handsome Trigs may start stuttering from the brambles on warm afternoons, and the earliest bush katydids appear. In a Brood XIX year — next due 2037 — this is the month the periodical cicadas would arrive instead, and nothing about the month would sound normal.

Jun.highlights: The chorus opens. The first cicadas start in the canopy late in the month and the Lesser Anglewing rasps after dark, well before the true katydids get going. Evenings are still much quieter than they will be in six weeks.

Jul.highlights: The true katydids arrive, usually in the first days of the month, and the night changes character completely. Cicadas hold the daylight hours. Everything is present but not yet at full volume.

Aug.highlights: PEAK. Every species is out at once and the night chorus becomes a single pulsing wall of sound — the loudest the property gets all year. The best month to try the tree-cricket thermometer against the station.

Sep.highlights: The handoff. Cicadas finish and the days go quiet; the katydids thin out; the cricket layer moves to the front. Cool nights start slowing everything down noticeably.

Oct.highlights: Down to crickets, and running slow. Watch the station on a clear night — Common True Katydids stop entirely below about 52°F, and up here that line gets crossed weeks earlier than it does in town.

Nov.highlights: A few field crickets on the warmest afternoons, then nothing. The first hard freeze ends the season outright.

Dec.highlights: Silent, and will stay silent until May.

_meta.notes: Water temperature estimates for Lake Sequoyah are derived from seasonal air temperature patterns adjusted for 2,800 ft elevation. Actual lake temperature varies — a $15 fishing thermometer on a line is the most reliable tool. Regulations should be verified annually at georgiawildlife.com before each season.
_meta.cardSummary: Lake Sequoyah · 0.3 mi from the property

lake.name: Lake Sequoyah
lake.history: Built 1928–1930 by Col. Sam Tate (Georgia Marble Company) as part of the Tate Mountain Estates resort development on Burnt Mountain. Dam completed April 1930. One of the highest-elevation warmwater fishing lakes in North Georgia.
lake.elevationNote: At 2,800 ft, this lake runs 8–12°F cooler than lowland Georgia lakes year-round. Spring warm-up is 4–6 weeks behind Atlanta-area lakes. Summer peak temps rarely exceed 78–80°F — an advantage for year-round fish activity compared to hot lowland lakes that suppress feeding in summer. Plan your seasonal timing around this.

regulations.source: Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division statewide freshwater regulations — verify annually at georgiawildlife.com
regulations.license: Georgia freshwater fishing license required age 16+. Available at georgiawildlife.com or local retailers.
regulations.catchAndRelease: During spawn (roughly late May–mid June at this elevation), consider voluntary C&R for bass on beds — removing spawning fish reduces next year's class.

waterTempGuide.note: These are estimated seasonal ranges for Lake Sequoyah at 2,800 ft. Use a clip-on thermometer for real readings. The cutoffs below drive all species behavior.

ranges.label: Dead of Winter
ranges.summary: All species sluggish. Bass suspended at deepest water. Worth coming back when a mild spell brings surface temps above 50°F.

ranges.label: Early Spring Stir
ranges.summary: Bass starting to move from deep winter haunts toward staging areas. Crappie beginning prespawn migration toward brush. Slow presentation critical — fish lethargic but can be tempted.

ranges.label: Pre-Spawn Prime
ranges.summary: Best sustained fishing of the year. Bass feeding aggressively before spawn — largest females most catchable now. Crappie moving to shallow brush. This window at Sequoyah runs roughly late April through May.

ranges.label: Spawn
ranges.summary: Bass on beds in 2–6 ft, highly visible and catchable but stressed. Crappie spawning near stumps and brush. Bluegill begin spawning. Consider C&R ethics during this window.

ranges.label: Post-Spawn / Early Summer
ranges.summary: Bass recovering from spawn, moving to structure in 8–15 ft. Feeding resumes. Bluegill very active on beds. Topwater productive at dawn. At 2,800 ft these temps rarely become oppressive.

ranges.label: Peak Summer
ranges.summary: Unlike lowland GA lakes, Sequoyah's elevation keeps summer temps below 80°F — fish remain reasonably active. Dawn and dusk are prime. Bass holding near shade, points, and any structure. Bluegill most active species.

ranges.label: Late Summer
ranges.summary: Temps beginning to moderate. Bass moving back toward shallower structure. Crappie transitioning to fall patterns. Consistent action for all three species.

ranges.label: Fall Feed
ranges.summary: Second-best window of the year, arguably the most fun. Bass feeding aggressively to pack on weight before winter — chasing baitfish in open water and shallows. Crappie pushing toward brush. Fast-moving lures effective.

ranges.label: Late Fall Slowdown
ranges.summary: Cooling quickly at elevation. Bass and crappie moving to deeper water. Slowing presentations. Late crappie can still be excellent at this lake on mild days.

seasonalCalendar.note: All months adjusted for Lake Sequoyah's 2,800 ft elevation. Lowland Georgia references (Atlanta, Lake Lanier) run 4–6 weeks ahead of these dates.

Jan.conditions: Cold — all species inactive in deep water. Save it for a warm spell above 50°F.

Feb.conditions: Still cold. Late February can produce crappie if temps break 50°F on sunny afternoons.

Mar.conditions: Water 45–55°F. Crappie starting to stir in deep brush. Bass pre-staging has begun but fish are lethargic.

Apr.conditions: Water rising through 52–62°F — prime pre-spawn bass window opens late April. Crappie active near brush. Best month to watch temps closely.

May.conditions: Best month of the year. Pre-spawn bass at peak aggression. Crappie spawn begins late May. Bluegill warming up. Worth being on the water this month.

Jun.conditions: Bass spawning mid-June at this elevation. Bluegill spawn in full swing — incredible fly fishing. Post-spawn bass recovering. Topwater dawn is excellent.

Jul.conditions: Peak summer but manageable at 2,800 ft. All species active, especially bluegill. Fish dawn/dusk. Bass on structure 8–12 ft.

Aug.conditions: Late summer — temps begin moderating. Bluegill still on beds or post-spawn. Bass starting early fall patterns. Consistent action all day.

Sep.conditions: Fall feed begins. Bass aggressively chasing baitfish. Crappie moving back to brush in shallows. One of the best months of the year.

Oct.conditions: Excellent fall action continuing. Bass topwater in mornings. Crappie near brush 4–10 ft. Temps dropping quickly at elevation — close the season strong.

Nov.conditions: Water cooling fast. Bass moving deep, slowing down. Crappie last good window on mild days. Dress warm.

Dec.conditions: Cold and slow. Rest up for next season.

bass.line: 10–15 lb fluorocarbon or 30–40 lb braid with fluoro leader
mustHaveLures: Ned rig — 3" Elaztech worm on 1/10 oz head (finesse days)
1/2 oz spinnerbait — white or chartreuse blade (overcast/stained)
1/16 oz tube jig — chartreuse, white, or pink
Bobby Garland Baby Shad on light jighead
Live minnow under slip float (most reliable)
Live cricket under small bobber (hardest to beat)
Foam spider or small popper on fly rod
Wax worm or small piece of nightcrawler

generalNotes: A basic $15 waterproof thermometer on a string is the highest-ROI fishing tool for this lake — knowing the exact water temp tells you where every species is and what they'll hit.
Polarized sunglasses for spotting bass beds and reading the water in the shallows.
Small tackle box is plenty for a mountain lake of this size — don't overpack.
Lake Sequoyah is a small reservoir. Walk the shoreline and probe the structure rather than covering open water.

historicalWaterTemp.note: Monthly typical lake water temp ranges for Lake Sequoyah (~2,800 ft elevation). Derived from NOAA 1991–2020 Climate Normals for Pickens County adjusted for elevation lapse rate (~4.7°F cooler than Jasper valley) and lake thermal inertia (water lags air 4–6 weeks warming, 2–3 weeks cooling). Not measured data — use as a planning guide; actual temps vary with weather.
historicalWaterTemp.dataSource: NOAA 1991–2020 Climate Normals, KJZP Pickens County Airport (1,535 ft); elevation-adjusted for 2,800 ft; thermal lag applied

species.name: Largemouth Bass
species.overview: The primary target species at Sequoyah. A small mountain reservoir at 2,800 ft means the population is not as dense as lowland impoundments, but the fish are healthy and well-fed. At this elevation the spawn runs 6–8 weeks behind Atlanta-area lakes — expect bedding fish in late May to mid-June rather than April.

tempPhases.behavior: Suspended near deepest water, metabolism near zero, almost no feeding. Not worth targeting.
tempPhases.bestApproach: If you must fish: 3/8 oz football jig dragged extremely slowly along bottom. Expect few bites.

tempPhases.behavior: Feeding aggressively to fuel the spawn. Staging near points, secondary channel edges, and structure adjacent to spawning flats. Largest females are most catchable in this window.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Squarebill crankbait along rocky points. Swimbait on a jighead along channel edges. Texas-rigged Senko or creature bait worked slowly. Spinnerbait in stained water or overcast days.

tempPhases.behavior: Males fanning beds in 2–6 ft on hard bottom near cover (stumps, rocks, laydowns). Females nearby, less aggressive. Highly visible — polarized sunglasses essential.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Finesse ned rig or drop shot worked on or near beds. Topwater popper early morning. Consider C&R for bedding fish.

tempPhases.behavior: Males guarding fry in shallows. Females recovering near first deep structure. At Sequoyah's elevation summer temps stay manageable — bass don't go as deep or shut down as hard as in lowland lakes.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Topwater (Whopper Plopper, popper) at dawn and dusk. Wacky-rigged Senko around any submerged stumps or wood. Ned rig on rocky points. Spinnerbait along weedline edges.

tempPhases.behavior: Most aggressive feeding of the year. Chasing shad and other baitfish in open water and over shallow flats. Fast-moving baits very effective. Often visibly blowing up on baitfish near the surface.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Topwater and medium-running crankbait. Chatterbait or vibrating jig. Lipless crankbait (Red Eye Shad). Follow shad activity — bass won't be far.

localTips: At 2,800 ft, the spawn runs 6–8 weeks later than Atlanta-area lakes. Don't expect bed fish before late May.
Stump fields and submerged timber (remnants of the original Clear Creek valley) are key structure.
Morning topwater in June and July will produce even through summer — the cooler water keeps bass surface-feeding longer into the day than lowland lakes.
The dam face and any rocky riprap are worth working in all seasons — shad and crayfish concentrate there.

species.name: Crappie
species.overview: Black and white crappie both likely present. At this elevation, crappie are slower to warm up in spring — the pre-spawn and spawn window runs about a month behind lowland lakes. They hold tightly to brush, stumps, and submerged wood year-round.

tempPhases.behavior: Suspended in deep water (10–20 ft) near brush piles or channel edges. Slow, but catchable with vertical jigging.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Drop a 1/32 oz jig or live minnow straight down into known brush. Virtually no lateral movement — dead still or barely twitching.

tempPhases.behavior: Moving from deep brush toward shallower staging areas. Feeding actively. One of the best consistent crappie windows.
tempPhases.depth: 6–12 ft on brush and secondary structure
tempPhases.bestApproach: 1/16–1/8 oz tube jig or curly tail grub in chartreuse, white, or pink. Slow horizontal retrieve near brush edges. Live minnow under a slip float is deadly.

tempPhases.behavior: Moves into shallow water (2–6 ft) near stumps, brush, and submerged wood to spawn. Very catchable — highly aggressive defenders.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Small tube jig or split-tail grub pitched to cover. Spider rig with multiple poles covering different depths. Live minnow is the most reliable spawn bait. This window at Sequoyah runs approximately late May to mid-June.

tempPhases.behavior: Moving to deeper, cooler water or suspending under shade near structure. Dawn and dusk feeding windows. Not absent — just harder to locate.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Vertical jigging near deep brush. Night fishing can be excellent — crappie attracted to lights. 1/16 oz jig in white or chartreuse.

tempPhases.behavior: Returns to shallower brush as temps cool. Feeding aggressively on shad. Often schooled up — if you catch one, there are more nearby.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Jig in natural shad colors — silver, white, grey. Live minnow under a bobber over brush. Casting and counting down to depth before retrieve.

localTips: Brush piles are everything for crappie. Any submerged wood, stumps, or artificial structure holds fish.
At 2,800 ft expect spawn 4–6 weeks later than lowland GA — late May to mid-June vs. April in Atlanta.
Crappie at elevation tend to be smaller but very concentrated in structure. Find the brush, find the fish.
A slip float rig with a live minnow 3–4 ft deep is the most consistently productive method for all seasons.

species.name: Bluegill
species.overview: The most accessible and arguably most fun species at Sequoyah. Abundant, aggressive, and willing to bite throughout the warmwater season. Excellent on ultralight tackle. Spawn multiple times per summer, making them catchable from late May through early September at this elevation.

tempPhases.behavior: Schooled tight in deeper, warmer water. Low activity. Can be caught but not worth targeting specifically.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Small jig or cricket on a drop shot near the bottom.

tempPhases.behavior: Moving shallower as temps rise. Appetite increasing. Edges of weed beds, rocky shallows, and dock areas.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Small in-line spinner (Rooster Tail). Live cricket or worm under a small bobber 2–3 ft deep. Light jig in chartreuse or white.

tempPhases.behavior: Colonies of males fanning visible circular beds in gravel or sandy shallows, 1–4 ft deep. Extremely aggressive — will strike almost anything near the bed. Multiple spawn batches run through summer.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Small popper on ultralight spinning or fly rod — one of the most fun freshwater experiences available. Live cricket or wax worm is also deadly. Small rubber spider fly or foam beetle. This window at Sequoyah runs June through early August.
tempPhases.note: Bluegill spawn multiple times per season when temps are right — you may catch this window 2–3 times from June through August.

tempPhases.behavior: Post-spawn fish scattered but still very active. Schooling near weed edges and structure, chasing small insects and nymphs.
tempPhases.bestApproach: Small soft plastic grub. Fly fishing with wooly bugger or small streamer. Worm under a bobber.

localTips: Bluegill are the best 'always something biting' option at Sequoyah. If bass and crappie are slow, bluegill will save the trip.
Fly fishing for bluegill on beds (June–July) is genuinely world-class fun on a small mountain lake — 5 or 6 weight rod, small poppers.
At 2,800 ft the spawn runs late — don't expect beds until early-to-mid June, about 4 weeks after lowland GA.
Crickets from any local bait shop are the single most reliable bluegill bait for all seasons.

_meta.purpose: The property's weeds — what to get after, when (before it seeds), and how. A field-journal domain, not a task list: the tone is 'worth getting after this before it seeds,' never 'N weeds due.' Every entry is a HYPOTHESIS until confirmed on the ground — each carries confidence + a needs-confirmation flag, and the Mama's-Perspective loop is how Mom settles it. As she answers, what we learn seeds MORE entries and MORE cards. AI may draft combat advice behind Paul's gate; Mom's surface + capture stay AI-free (ask-path vs capture-path).

weeds.summary: What's worth getting after — and when, before it seeds
weeds.intro: A running note on the weeds that turn up on the property — the ones worth getting after before they set seed, with a plain read on how to handle each. Everything here starts as a best guess from a photo and gets settled on the ground: the surest fix for most weeds is timing, and the surest way to know what we're looking at is a good look when it seeds.

weeds.name: Crabgrass
weeds.lookFor: A low grass that spreads flat in a star from a central point, rather than growing upright in a clump. Light green, wider blades held out near the ground. Turns up in thin, scalped, or bare patches in the heat of summer.
weeds.habit: Summer annual — sprouts each spring from seed, races through the summer, and dies at the first frost. It does its damage by seeding heavily before it goes, so next year's crop is set now.

seedTiming.note: It throws unmistakable finger-like seed spikes in late summer. That's both the tell that it really is crabgrass and the last good moment to pull or cut it before it drops next year's seed.

combat: The real defense is a thick fescue turf — crabgrass only gets a foothold in thin, bare, or scalped spots. Mow high (3–3.5") and overseed thin areas every September so it has nowhere to start.
Pull or dig the isolated plants before the seed-heads open — the whole plant lifts from one crown.
If it's widespread, next year's lever is a spring pre-emergent, laid down before the soil warms (~55°F, about mid-March here). It stops the seed from sprouting; little helps once it's already up.
Don't feed the lawn in high summer — it favors the crabgrass over the fescue.

momConfirm.confirmBy: the finger-like seed spikes in late summer

weeds.notes: First surfaced as the low, spreading 'second grass' in the turf and meadow photos (2026-07-20). Recorded here as inferred, pending Mom's confirmation on the ground.
weeds._zoneRemapNote: 2026-09-01: was ['fairway','fairway-fringe']. fairway-fringe resolves deterministically (-> fairway-border -> the-green-ring). 'fairway' does NOT: that polygon was retired and its ground SPLIT into the-turf and the-meadow, so both are listed. THIS IS THE FAITHFUL UNION, NOT A NARROWING — the original claim covered all of that ground. Do not read three zones as three observations.

weeds.name: Japanese stiltgrass
weeds.lookFor: A low, sprawling grass that lies across the ground in loose mats rather than standing up. Short lance-shaped leaves, an inch or two long, each with a tell-tale pale, silvery stripe running slightly off-center down the middle. Loves shade and damp ground along the woods edge.
weeds.habit: A summer annual — comes up thick each year from seed, sprawls all summer, and dies at frost. It's one of the most aggressive shade invasives in the Southeast; a patch left alone carpets the ground and crowds native growth out.

seedTiming.note: It sets seed in late summer, just before frost, and a single season's seed can carpet the ground for years. Getting after it before it seeds is the whole game.

combat: It's shallow-rooted — a patch pulls up in easy handfuls, or a string-trimmer / mow knocks it down. The key is doing it in late summer, before the seed ripens.
Because it reseeds so heavily, one clearing isn't enough — stay after the same spots for a few years to run the seed bank down.
Shade and a thick native groundcover are its enemies; bare, disturbed, damp ground is where it takes hold.
For a heavy stand, a spring pre-emergent (same timing as for crabgrass) stops the seed from sprouting.

momConfirm.confirmBy: the pale silvery stripe down each leaf, and how easily a whole mat pulls up

weeds.notes: The dominant sprawling grass in the woodland-edge photos (7/20). Recorded inferred pending confirmation on the ground.

weeds.name: Beggar's lice (tick-trefoil)
weeds.lookFor: Wiry, thin, sprawling stems with small pink-purple pea flowers, and leaves in threes (a leaflet trio). After it flowers it forms little flat, triangular seed segments in a chain — the ones that stick to your clothes and the dog by the dozen.
weeds.habit: A native legume of woodland edges — not a bully like the stiltgrass. The nuisance is entirely the seeds: those flat triangular segments are covered in tiny hooks and hitch a ride on anything that brushes past, which is exactly how it spreads.

seedTiming.window: Late summer — before the pods ripen
seedTiming.note: Cut or pull the flowering stems before the little triangular pods dry and start sticking. Once they're ripe, every pass through a patch plants next year's crop somewhere new.

combat: Pull or cut the stems while it's flowering, before the sticky pods set — that's the one move that matters.
It's a native and not aggressive, so there's no need to go to war with it — just keep it cut back along the paths where the seeds catch you.
A thick edge of taller native growth shades it down over time.

momConfirm.confirmBy: whether the little flat triangular seeds stick to your clothes

weeds.notes: The pink-flowered, sticky-seeded plant in the 7/20 photos. Recorded inferred pending confirmation.

weeds.name: Virginia creeper
weeds.lookFor: A climbing vine whose leaves each have FIVE leaflets spreading from one point, like fingers on a hand, with toothed edges. Note the five — that's what tells it apart from poison ivy, which always has three. Turns brilliant red in fall.
weeds.habit: A native vine, and a good one for wildlife — birds take the dark berries. It's only a 'weed' where it climbs somewhere you don't want it: up the house, into a shrub, or across a bed.

seedTiming.window: Not seed-driven — manage where it climbs
