seedTiming.note: No urgent seed window here; it spreads mostly by running and rooting. The move is to cut it back wherever it's climbing into something before the vine gets woody and hard to pull.

combat: Where it's not bothering anything, leave it — it's native and feeds the birds.
Where it climbs the house or into a shrub, cut it at the base and pull the young runners; the roots come up fairly easily when the plant is young.
Five leaflets, not three — worth being sure before pulling, so it isn't confused with poison ivy nearby.

momConfirm.confirmBy: counting five leaflets on a leaf (poison ivy has three)

weeds.notes: The five-leaflet vine in the 7/20 photos. Native; recorded here because Paul flagged it. Inferred pending confirmation.

weeds.name: Wild violet

weeds.habit: A tough native spring wildflower that many people are happy to keep as a groundcover — it feeds early pollinators. It earns the 'weed' label mostly in a tidy lawn, where its rhizomes make it hard to be rid of.

seedTiming.note: Not a get-it-before-it-seeds case — it's a perennial that persists on its roots. Spring, when the purple flowers are out, is simply the easiest time to be sure of what it is.

combat: If it's welcome as a groundcover, nothing to do — it's a native and a pollinator plant.
Where it's unwanted in turf, dig the whole rhizome; mowing and pulling tops alone won't finish it.
Wait for the spring flowers to confirm it before treating anything.

hardiness.elevationAdjustedZone: 6b to 7a (mid-slope and open positions); 6a possible in confirmed frost pockets
hardiness.explanation: Pickens County is officially USDA Zone 7b based on valley-floor stations. At a confirmed elevation of 2,873 ft — approximately 1,338 ft above the KJZP reference station — the standard environmental lapse rate (3.5–5.5°F per 1,000 ft) implies approximately 5–8°F cooler average winter minimum than the valley. This pushes the property solidly into Zone 6b (−5 to 0°F minimum) on open mid-slope positions, and potentially Zone 6a (−10 to −5°F) in confirmed frost pockets on calm clear nights. Plan for Zone 6b as your baseline and treat any hollow or low-lying area as Zone 6a.
hardiness.coldAirDrainageEffect_F: 8–15°F colder in valley bottoms / hollows on calm clear nights vs. mid-slope

frostDates.source: NOAA 1991–2020 Climate Normals for Jasper GA, elevation-adjusted for confirmed 1,338 ft above KJZP (2,873 ft vs 1,535 ft)

valleyFloor_KJZP.note: Official climate-normal dates for the Jasper/KJZP station (1,535 ft) — your baseline reference.

atPropertyElevation.note: Adjusted ~+10 days spring / -10 days fall for confirmed 1,338 ft additional elevation (using 7 days per 1,000 ft lapse). Applies to open mid-slope positions. Add another 5–14 days for any beds in frost pockets.

frostDates.frostPocketWarning: Any hollow, draw, or low-lying area where cold air pools on calm nights can experience frost 1–4 weeks earlier in fall and later in spring than the open mid-slope estimates above. At nearly 3,000 ft, these pockets should be treated as Zone 6a.

climate.precipitationNotes: 57 in/yr at valley station. Orographic lift on mountain slopes typically adds 5–15% over the valley reading — Church Mountain at ~2,873 ft likely receives 62–68 in/yr. Well distributed year-round with slight spring peak (Mar–May). Afternoon convective thunderstorms common Jun–Aug.

temperature.extremeWinterLow_F: Zone 6b baseline — expect lows of −5 to 0°F in hard winters at mid-slope; frost pockets may briefly reach −10°F

humidity.summer: High — 70–90% RH June–September. At elevation, afternoon fog and cloud immersion is possible, which raises fungal pressure (boxwood blight, powdery mildew). Prioritize air circulation in plantings.
humidity.fallWinter: Moderate — drier, lower humidity; best season for outdoor work and soil amendments

wind.summer: Light and variable; primarily SW; afternoon thunderstorm outflow can produce sudden strong gusts. Ridge and exposed positions get more wind than valley.
wind.winter: NW to NE; cold Canadian air masses; exposed ridge positions at nearly 3,000 ft get significant wind chill and evergreen desiccation — more severe than valley readings suggest
wind.iceStormRisk: Moderate to high — Pickens County sits in the Appalachian cold-air damming zone; at 2,873 ft, ice and snow accumulation will be heavier and more persistent than in the valley. 3–5 ice/snow events per winter typical.
wind.snowfall_in_avg: 5–10 in/yr on average; individual storms can bring 6–12 in but most winters see modest accumulation. NOAA 1991–2020 normals show Blairsville (1,900 ft) averaging 3.1 in/yr — the property at 2,873 ft gets somewhat more but North Georgia remains well below Appalachian snowbelt averages.

climate.growingSeasonNotes: At ~2,873 ft, the growing season is meaningfully shorter than the valley — approximately 167 days at mid-slope. Wait until late May to plant tender annuals. Fall harvest window closes in late September at exposed positions. Summer temperatures are pleasantly cooler than Atlanta by 10–15°F.

soils.seriesNote: INFERRED, not tested. Cecil and Pacolet were removed 2026-07-25: both are thermic Piedmont series capped near 900 ft elevation and do not occur in this county's soil survey, so they cannot be right for a 2,873 ft Blue Ridge site. The series listed now are the mesic, higher-elevation Blue Ridge candidates (Ashe, Edneyville and Porters are shallow, coarse-loamy Inceptisols; Tallapoosa is a shallow Hapludult mapped nearby). Which one is actually underfoot is unconfirmed until the W9 soil test returns a texture result. See .plans/2026-07-25-soil-sampling-plan.md.
soils.parentMaterial: Residuum weathered from high-grade metamorphic and igneous rock — mica gneiss, mica schist, granodiorite. Typical of the Southern Appalachian Blue Ridge.
soils.texture: Sandy loam to loam surface over a coarse, micaceous subsoil; on these Blue Ridge slopes the soil is typically shallow, with weathered rock within roughly 20 inches. Well to excessively drained. The governing constraint here is shallow rooting depth and summer drought stress on a steep slope, NOT perched water over clay (the clay-subsoil/argillic story belongs to the Piedmont series that were wrongly listed before 2026-07-25 and does not apply at this elevation). Unconfirmed until the W9 soil test.
soils.structure: Moderate granular structure when in good health; can become compacted and crusting when depleted of organic matter or heavily trafficked.

pH.nativeRange: Likely 4.5-5.5 (acidic), but INFERRED from regional Blue Ridge soils - NO on-site soil test has ever been run, so treat this as a hypothesis, not a measurement. The W9 soil test will replace it with real per-zone numbers.

plantingTargets.acidLovers: 4.5–5.5 — azaleas, rhododendrons, mountain laurel, blueberries; your native soil is ideal unlimed
plantingTargets.generalShrubsAndTrees: 5.5–6.5 — dogwood, hydrangea, boxwood, holly, Japanese maple; may need light liming
plantingTargets.vegetables: 6.0–6.8 — may need liming for vegetable gardens
plantingTargets.turf: 6.0–6.5 — likely needs liming if establishing lawn areas

pH.soilTestRecommendation: Get a UGA Extension soil test for each distinct planting area before adding any amendments. $9 basic test through Pickens County Extension Office (706-253-8840). Tests for pH, P, K, Ca, Mg and give lime/fertilizer recommendations.

drainage.onSlopes: Well-drained to excessively drained — water moves through quickly; drought stress risk in summer
drainage.flatAreas: On the few flatter benches, check drainage by digging a 12-inch hole and watching it after rain before planting anything moisture-sensitive. (The old 'perched water over clay subsoil' warning was tied to the mis-listed Piedmont series and likely overstates the risk on these coarse, shallow soils.)
drainage.lowAreas: Potential for seasonal wet spots — check before planting moisture-sensitive species

organicMatter.native: Low to moderate on slopes; naturally depleted by erosion and rapid decomposition in warm humid climate
organicMatter.improvement: Annual additions of leaf mulch and compost are the single highest-return investment for mountain garden soil. 2–3 inch mulch layer year-round on all beds.

nutrients.potassium: Moderate to high from mica weathering — K deficiency uncommon
nutrients.phosphorus: Often low-to-medium; acidic soils fix P in unavailable forms. Test before adding P fertilizer.
nutrients.calcium_magnesium: Often low due to acidity; liming with dolomitic limestone raises pH and simultaneously adds Ca and Mg
nutrients.nitrogen: Low; organic matter additions and slow-release fertilizers most appropriate

soils.rockContent: Moderate to high — mica schist and gneiss parent material means rocks, chert, and occasionally large boulders near the surface. Raised beds may be preferable for intensive vegetable gardening.

microclimate.overview: At ~2,873 ft, Church Mountain Road sits well into Blue Ridge mountain territory. The combination of elevation, slope aspect, and topographic position (ridge vs. draw vs. mid-slope vs. valley bottom) can create temperature differences of 15–20°F across a single property on a calm clear night. This elevation is meaningfully colder, snowier, and windier than Jasper town — plan accordingly.
microclimate.elevationEffect: At 1,338 ft above the KJZP valley station, the property runs approximately 5–8°F cooler in average winter minimums. Summer highs are 8–12°F cooler than Atlanta, making it a genuine mountain climate. Spring green-up 10–14 days later than Jasper valley; fall color 2–3 weeks earlier.

south_southwest.bestFor: Heat-loving vegetables, sun-tolerant ornamentals, fruit trees
south_southwest.caution: High summer heat stress — water demands elevated; Japanese maple and azalea leaf scorch more likely here

north_northeast.character: Coolest and moistest — at this elevation, north-facing slopes can hold snow and frost significantly longer
north_northeast.bestFor: Azaleas, rhododendrons, mountain laurel, ferns, wildflowers, hostas
north_northeast.caution: Frost lingers later in spring; fungal disease (anthracnose, root rot) elevated by persistent moisture and shade

east.character: Morning sun, afternoon shade — the balanced optimum
east.bestFor: Hydrangeas, dogwoods, most ornamentals; broadest compatible plant list
east.caution: None significant — generally most favorable orientation for the plant list you have

west.character: Afternoon sun and heat exposure; wind exposure from prevailing SW breezes is more pronounced at this elevation
west.caution: High afternoon water stress in summer; significant wind exposure

thermalBelt.description: Mid-slope positions approximately 100–400 ft above the valley floor are typically the frost-safest positions on any mountain property. Cold air drains downhill on calm clear nights and pools in the valley while the mid-slope stays warmer.
thermalBelt.estimatedAdvantage_F: 3–8°F warmer than valley bottom on calm clear nights
thermalBelt.implication: Your best beds for borderline-hardy plants are on the middle slope, not the valley bottom or the exposed ridge top.

frostPockets.description: Any topographic low — hollow, draw, depression, base of a slope — is a frost pocket. At nearly 3,000 ft, frost pockets can be extreme.
frostPockets.identification: On a clear calm night in spring or fall, use a thermometer to compare your low spots vs. mid-slope. A 10°F difference is not uncommon.
frostPockets.gardeningImplication: Do not plant marginally-hardy species in known frost pockets. Good uses for frost pockets: native woodland species, hardy ferns, cold-tolerant vegetables.

orographicPrecipitation.description: At 2,873 ft, Church Mountain is well into orographic lift territory. Moisture-laden air rises and cools against the mountain, dropping significantly more rain and snow than the valley.
orographicPrecipitation.implication: Drainage is critical. Hillside beds drain quickly but lower/flat areas may stay wetter than expected. Winter snow accumulation will be heavier and linger longer than in Jasper town.

southFacingClearing.description: The house sits at the top of a large open south-facing open clearing, visible in satellite imagery. This is the dominant microclimate feature of the property.
southFacingClearing.solarGain: Maximum solar gain on the south face of the house year-round. South-facing glass and south-side plantings will receive full unobstructed sun from late morning through afternoon.
southFacingClearing.snowMelt: Snow and frost clear significantly faster on the clearing and south-facing beds than on any forested or north-facing areas of the property.
southFacingClearing.temperatureEffect: The open clearing warms quickly on sunny days — the clearing and south beds will run 5–10°F warmer than the surrounding forest on calm sunny afternoons.
southFacingClearing.windExposure: The open clearing provides less wind shelter than a forested setting. Summer SW breezes and winter NW winds will be more noticeable on the south face than in sheltered forest positions.
southFacingClearing.frostBehavior: Despite the solar advantage, the open clearing can radiate heat rapidly on calm clear nights — watch for radiative frost even when mid-slope forested areas stay frost-free.
southFacingClearing.gardeningImplication: South beds along the house foundation are the warmest, most sun-rich positions on the property — ideal for vegetables, heat-loving perennials, and marginally hardy plants that need the extra warmth. Avoid moisture-sensitive plants that can't handle afternoon heat at this aspect.

story._meta: The property card's almanac page — the lead paragraph and the surface-fact callouts. MOVED HERE 2026-09-03 (C4 5c / C5 7b): these were typed into engine JS (renderProperty) and named this place from inside the engine; canon owns them now and the renderer reads `story`. Bodies may carry inline HTML links. An estate with no `story` renders no lead and no callouts.
story.lead: The house sits at 2,873 feet on a south-facing shoulder of the Blue Ridge in Pickens County — land that was Cherokee Nation until 1838 and that became Tate Mountain Estates a century later, when Col. Sam Tate raised Lake Sequoyah a quarter-mile down the hill. The soil is Hayesville and Cecil and Pacolet — the red-clay subsoil and mica-flecked loam that this part of the Appalachians has been weathering out of gneiss and schist for a long time. Rain that falls on the fairway drains east into the headwaters of the Etowah; on clear nights the sky reads Bortle 3, one tier shy of the darkest in Georgia. It is a small piece of a large place, and the almanac that follows is an attempt to keep track of it.

callouts.heading: Tate Mountain Estates
callouts.bodyHtml: The house stands inside Tate Mountain Estates, the mountain development Col. Sam Tate of the Georgia Marble Company laid out in 1928. He raised Lake Sequoyah at the heart of it — naming it for the Cherokee silversmith who invented the syllabary in the 1820s — and built the Connahaynee Lodge atop Burnt Mountain at 3,300 feet: thirty rooms, marble baths, American chestnut logs. The Depression took the company into bankruptcy in 1934, and a basement fire took the lodge in March of 1946. The lake and the road grid are what remained. Fernwood is what this small piece of it is called.

callouts.heading: On Cherokee land
callouts.bodyHtml: This ground was Cherokee Nation territory from 1793 until the 1838 Removal. Talking Rock Creek, six miles east, ran through Sanderstown — the first community along the creek, founded by the Cherokee Sanders brothers — and through Taloney, where a day school called the Carmel Mission ran from 1819 until Removal. The Federal Road crossed the creek at the ford where Hwy 136 crosses now; the same site became Fort Newman, the stockade that held local Cherokee in 1838. The white oak, ramps, sochan, and ginseng on this mountainside were tended for thousands of years before there was a survey line. The Eastern Band's Center for Cherokee Plants still keeps that seedwork going in western North Carolina.

callouts.heading: The original Appalachian Trail
callouts.bodyHtml: From 1937 to 1958 the Appalachian Trail ended on Mount Oglethorpe, the high point of Pickens County and the same ridge as this house. Col. Sam Tate engineered the southern routing himself, bringing the trail through his private land to draw foot traffic up to the resort. The terminus moved thirteen miles northeast to Springer Mountain in 1958 after logging, chicken ranching, and a gravel road brought vandalism to the summit. Eagles Rest Park preserves the original site.

callouts.heading: A Unionist county
callouts.bodyHtml: The Union flag flew over the Pickens courthouse for nearly a month after Georgia seceded in 1861; the state government had to demand its removal. This county sits north of the old cotton line — small subsistence farms, few enslaved people, more Unionist sentiment than plantation economy. Six companies went to the Confederacy and one — Company D of the 1st Georgia Infantry Battalion — went to the Union Army, and a Pickens militia cavalry unit guided Sherman around Confederate positions during the Atlanta Campaign.

callouts.heading: Worked marble, eight hundred AD
callouts.bodyHtml: The Pickens marble deposit runs five to seven miles long and up to two thousand feet deep. Native peoples worked it as far back as 800 AD — a thousand years before Henry Fitzsimmons opened the first commercial quarry in the 1830s and the Tate family organized the Georgia Marble Company in 1884. About sixty percent of the monuments in Washington use it.

callouts.heading: A Bortle 3 sky
callouts.bodyHtml: The night sky here reads Bortle 3 on the nine-step scale that runs from inner-city orange (9) to the rare unpolluted dark of a desert sky (1). Stephen C. Foster State Park, in the Okefenokee, is Bortle 2 — the only IDA-certified dark-sky site in Georgia — which puts this ridge one tier off the darkest sky the state offers. The Milky Way is visible overhead from May through September on a clear moonless night.

callouts.heading: Keystone plants for the Blue Ridge
callouts.bodyHtml: A handful of native plant genera do a disproportionate share of the ecological work in this ecoregion. Oaks support more than 400 species of butterfly and moth caterpillars on their leaves; willows around 300; cherries around 200; blueberries and goldenrods carry the herbaceous layer. Those caterpillars are what the warblers and chickadees feed to their nestlings in May and June. The mature oak-hickory forest around the house is doing real work in that food chain.

callouts.heading: Outdoor burning, by season
callouts.bodyHtml: Georgia's state outdoor-burning ban runs May 1 through September 30 statewide — no permits issued, no open burning of yard debris. The rest of the year, burns require a permit from the Georgia Forestry Commission at gatrees.org. The ban is an air-quality rule, not a fire-danger rule; it covers the months when ground-level ozone pushes hardest.

callouts.heading: Homegrown National Park
callouts.bodyHtml: Doug Tallamy's Homegrown National Park is a grassroots project that asks landowners to register native habitat — any size, any condition — on a single national map. The math is that private land in aggregate dwarfs every public preserve combined, and that biodiversity recovery is mostly a matter of what gets planted at home. The property qualifies on the strength of the existing mature forest alone.

turf.summary: Two regimes on the open clearing — kept turf and natural meadow
turf.intro: The open south-facing clearing below the house is the property's defining ground — and it's run as two different things at once. The part nearest the house is kept as lush turf, mowed regularly. The rest is let go as meadow, cut back hard just once a year and otherwise left to grow tall, loose, and full of wildflowers. The contrast is deliberate: a crisp green turf reading against a seed-headed, pollinator-fed meadow.

regimes.label: The lush turf
regimes.summary: For a lush, mowed turf at 2,873 ft the grass is turf-type tall fescue — a cool-season bunchgrass, and UGA's standard answer for the North Georgia mountains. The summers here run too cool for Bermuda and far too humid for the creeping bentgrass a golf green would use; that bentgrass is a maintenance trap for a home lawn — disease-prone in the humidity, near-daily mowing, heavy fungicide. (And the autumn bentgrass Mom flagged is a different plant entirely — a native meadow grass, not a turf.) Fescue grows in clumps rather than running, so it never knits over bare spots on its own: the turf stays full by overseeding thin areas every fall.
essentials: Mow high — 3 to 3.5 inches — and raise to 3.5–4″ through the June–August heat. Never take more than a third of the blade at once, and leave the clippings.
Overseed thin spots every September — the one window that matters. Fall seeding roots through two cool seasons before it faces summer; spring seeding rarely survives.
Lime to bring the acidic native soil (pH 4.5–5.5) toward 6.0–6.5. Size it to a UGA soil test and apply in fall — the single biggest lever on turf color.
Water deeply, about 1″ a week in summer drought, early in the morning. The open south face dries faster than anywhere else on the property.
Watch for brown patch in humid heat — answer it with morning watering, a higher cut, and no summer nitrogen before reaching for a fungicide.

regimes.label: The meadow
regimes.summary: Beyond the turf, the rest of the clearing is run the natural way — as meadow. This is where the native warm-season bunchgrasses belong: little bluestem, big bluestem, indiangrass, switchgrass, and the autumn bentgrass Mom flagged, threaded through with wildflowers. It asks almost nothing — no lime, no fertilizer, no weekly mowing — and gives back cover and seed for birds and a long pollinator season.
essentials: Mow once a year in late winter (late February), down to 4–6 inches — never lower — to clear last year's growth before the new season and before ground-nesting birds get going.
In the first year of a new seeding, mow every 4–6 weeks at that height to hold back annual weeds while the slow native perennials root in, then drop to the once-a-year cut.
Leave the soil acidic and unfed — feeding a meadow favors weeds and floppy growth over the wildflowers you want.
The first move in the fringe may simply be to stop mowing and see what native grass (like purpletop) is already there.

_meta._aliasesNote: `aliases[]` — added 2026-09-01 at fleet lap 2, Paul-approved. What a machine is CALLED in speech, beyond its name: dictation variants ('Beloris' for Bolores — his own, from the lap-1 chronicle), short forms ('DR200'), and words the record simply does not contain ('fridge' where the record says 'refrigerator'). ⭐ WHY IT EXISTS: beat 0 could only ever resolve vocabulary the record happened to hold, so the resolver worked right up until Paul used his own word for something — measured at lap 2 when 'the fridge is making noise' resolved to a leaf blower. ⭐ THE DESIGN RULE, and it is the counter-intuitive half: where two machines genuinely share a word, BOTH carry it, so the tool goes AMBIGUOUS and ASKS rather than silently picking. 'truck' is on the F-150 AND on Bolores; 'bike' is on both motorcycles. An alias that resolves a coin-flip is worse than no alias. ⚠️ PROVENANCE: only 'Beloris' and 'DR200' come from Paul's own speech; the rest were proposed by the lap and are his to correct — these are HIS words for HIS machines, and the record should not invent them. Resolver treats aliases as a STRONG field (tools/vehicle-brief.py).

maintenance.coils: Vacuum the condenser coils once or twice a year. On a bottom-freezer LG they sit behind the lower back panel or behind the toe grille at the floor. Dust on the coils is the single most common reason a fridge runs warm and works harder than it needs to.
maintenance.temperature: 37°F in the refrigerator and 0°F in the freezer are the numbers to hold. A fridge thermometer on a shelf is the cheap way to know — the dial setting is not a reading.
maintenance.doorSeal: Wipe the door gaskets a few times a year and check the seal by closing the door on a dollar bill — if it slides out with no drag, that stretch of gasket is letting warm air in. On a bottom-freezer the drawer gasket is the one that gets missed.
maintenance.iceMaker: It works today, and that is worth keeping. The usual failures are the fill tube freezing over and the inlet valve weakening with age — both show up first as small or hollow cubes rather than as a dead maker. If ice slows down, that is the signal, not the silence.
maintenance.waterFilter: [UNCONFIRMED — verify before relying on this] OPEN QUESTION — do not buy a filter on this line alone. Because there is no water dispenser, this unit may carry no internal water filter at all, or an inline one on the supply behind the fridge. Worth a look behind the unit before assuming either.
maintenance.waterLine: An ice maker means there is a water line running to the fridge even without a dispenser. The shutoff behind or below the unit is the thing to know the location of before it is ever needed in a hurry.

maintenance.gfciTest: The GFI circuits (kitchen counter, upstairs, stairway, and the hard-to-read 30) protect people, and they can fail quietly. Press the TEST button on each GFCI outlet every few months — it should click dead, then reset.

A two-minute flip test settles both, and confirms the 240 V pairs. A booster pump, if that's what 28 is, means the water supply has pressure help worth putting in this record.
maintenance.spares: A spare 15 A and 20 A Homeline (HOM) single-pole breaker in a drawer costs a few dollars and saves a hardware-store run during an outage. Match the HOM type — the bus won't take other brands.
